Hector's play becomes real campaigning as the novel follows him through the wars of religion that tore Europe apart. Henty mixes battles, sieges, and personal courage in his usual brisk style. Young readers get both an adventure story and a plain introduction to a war that shaped modern Europe.
5102-the-path-of-a-star:
Mrs. Everard Cotes's Path of a Star opens on an actress entering a room, pushing the portiere aside with a curved hand and gracefully separated fingers. Her body follows after an instant's poised hesitation, head thrust forward, eyes inquiring, a tentative smile on her face, though she knows precisely who waits there.

She crosses quickly, the train of her luxurious morning gown folding with audacity as she bends over Laura Filbert on a bamboo sofa and cries, You poor thing. The novel follows an actress's career and loves with theatrical immediacy. Readers get a story of the stage, where performance and private feeling constantly trade places.
566-the-history-of-the-thirty-years-war:
Friedrich Schiller narrates the Thirty Years' War in this history, translated by A. J. W. Morrison. Schiller traces the Reformation's effects, the revolt of Matthias, the Bohemian rising, and the clash of Union and League, with lucidity and impartial judgment. His preface praises his own gift for history as well as drama.

Chapters move from emperors and electors to armies and treaties, showing how faith and power tore Europe apart. Schiller writes as a dramatist turned historian, keen on character and cause. The work endures as a classic popular history, clear, grave, and humane.
5713-tales-of-war:
Lord Dunsany's Tales of War, published in 1918, gathers short pieces written during the First World War, many in the voice of soldiers and villagers. The opening prayer of the men of Daleswood tells of a hill village with only twenty houses. Thirty men between sixteen and forty-five lived there. All of them went to war together in the same battalion. That small scale gives the book its power.

Dunsany writes with a poet's brevity, letting a single image or farewell carry the weight of loss. Readers meet trenches, home villages, and the strange quiet between battles, rendered without long battle scenes. The collection suits readers of war literature who prefer short, haunting sketches to full novels, and it preserves how one well-known fantasist faced a real war.
5981-the-boy-scouts-in-front-of-warsaw-o:
Colonel George Durston opens on 5 August with Warsaw fallen, brilliant and beautiful, now torn by bombs, wrecked by shells, and left in ruins. Her people seem to have vanished in the two days since the city was taken, while wealthy citizens shelter in the lower town and invaders take the grand houses.

Warsaw lies on a plain by the Vistula, its streets twisted like snakes, its houses very old. Into this wreckage come the Boy Scouts, in the twentieth volume of the series. Durston sets a boys' adventure against real war damage, where courage must serve amid deserted streets and broken palaces.
605-pellucidar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs returns to the hollow Earth in this sequel to At the Earth's Core. A letter from Algiers lures the narrator from lion hunting in Africa back to Pellucidar, where David Innes fights Hooja's cutthroats, cave prisons, and raids. Chapters race from lost wanderings to conquest and peace.

Burroughs writes at his usual gallop, with chutes, captures, kidnappings, and escapes. The inner world's eternal sun and strange beasts frame each peril. The book charms as a brisk continuation, where a modern hero must win a stone-age world by nerve and friendship.
6386-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Suetonius himself was son of a Roman knight who commanded a legion for Otho at the battle that gave Vitellius the empire. He was born near the close of Vespasian's reign, his translator's preface notes. His first life, Caius Julius Caesar the Divine, loses his father at sixteen. Named high priest of Jupiter the next year, he repudiates a wealthy equestrian bride, Cossutia, contracted as a boy. He marries Cornelia, daughter of four times consul Cinna, and has a daughter Julia.

Resisting dictator Sylla's efforts to make him divorce Cornelia, Caesar suffers penalty and exile's shadow before his rise. Later he reforms the calendar to three hundred and sixty-five days, with an intercalary day every fourth year. Inserting two months so the year begins on January's calends, he makes a fifteen month year. Suetonius writes Caesar as ambition, law, and family honour in one life, from priesthood to calendar.
6604-two-months-in-the-camp-of-big-bear:
Theresa Gowanlock and Theresa Delaney tell, in their own words, two months spent in the camp of Big Bear during the North-West troubles. Their chapters run from leaving Ontario and the fight at Battleford to the massacre, the fall of Fort Pitt, and life as captives cooking for a large family. Hope almost deferred gives way, at last, to rescue and the road home.

A second part adds Gowanlock's youth, marriage, and later life, with notes on Father Fafard and the Saskatchewan stream. The tone is plain and direct, with no polish to hide fear or grief. Two Months in the Camp of Big Bear is a stark, first-hand account of war, captivity, and survival on the Canadian plains.
6673-young-knights-of-the-empire-their-c:
Robert Baden-Powell, founder of the scouts, offers further yarns for boy-men, with the scout code at their heart. His foreword warns that yarns alone are of little worth unless the ideas in them are put into daily, habitual practice. Boys, he says, need encouragement to live the code, not just to hear it.

The tales that follow show self-education in character and good citizenship, step by step as in Scouting for Boys. Courage, loyalty, thrift, and service run through each story. Young Knights of the Empire is a plain, earnest scout book from 1917, made to turn reading into doing.
6870-why-we-are-at-war:
Woodrow Wilson's Why We Are at War gathers his messages to Congress from January to April 1917. It adds his war proclamation of April 6 and his message to the American people of April 15. Harper published the book in May 1917. It runs from a world league for peace and the severance of ties with Germany. Then it moves to a request for power and the stark message that war must be accepted.

Publishers note they sought approval for the title and captions, and present these historic documents in collected form as a service of lasting worth. Wilson's prose is grave, idealistic, and direct. Why We Are at War is a key primary source on America's entry into the Great War.
7189-a-short-history-of-the-great-war:
A. F. Pollard, professor of English history at the University of London, tells the Great War in one short volume with nineteen maps, first published in 1920. His chapters run from the breach of the peace and the German invasion through Russia's moves and war on and beyond the seas. Then comes the fixing of the Western Front, two winters of war, and the failure of the Allied offensive.

Pollard carries the tale on to the defeat of Russia and the climax of German success. A second German offensive in the west meets the Allied counter-offensive, with the Balkans and politics alongside the fighting. The book aims at a clear, compact account for readers who want the whole war in view without a shelf of volumes. Maps help the reader hold each front in mind.
7411-an-art-lovers-guide-to-the-expositi:
Sheldon Cheney wrote this guide for visitors to San Francisco's great exposition of 1915, the Panama-Pacific fair that celebrated the city rebuilt after the earthquake. He explains the architecture, sculpture, and mural paintings court by court: the Court of the Universe, the Court of the Four Seasons, the Tower of Jewels, and the palaces facing the Marina. The Palace of Machinery and the Festival Hall get their own chapters.

Cheney writes for the less practiced eye, praising and criticizing in terms a lay visitor can use. He admits he claims no special power of artistic judgment, only the wish to help others see new beauties. A final guide for study in the art gallery turns a day's visit into a course. The book now doubles as a souvenir of a vanished fair.
7435-springhaven-a-tale-of-the-great-war:
R. D. Blackmore published Springhaven in 1887, and its great war is not the war of his own century's end but the Napoleonic struggle. In the days when England trusted mainly to the vigor of one man against a world of enemies, the quiet village of Springhaven lay on a coast in great peril. Yet the village, sheltered by a bold point called Haven-head, kept its tranquil ways.

The novel opens when the ship comes home, and follows the village as war presses on its fishermen, smugglers, and families. Blackmore, author of Lorna Doone, writes with the same love of the West Country coast and its people. Springhaven is a tale of a small place holding its character while history storms offshore, with the sea itself as a constant presence.
7803-the-story-of-sugar:
Sara Ware Bassett's The Story of Sugar, pictured by C. P. Gray, follows boys at Colversham through sugaring off, a refinery visit, and a family tangle. Bobbie is called from algebra to play, Van springs a surprise, mutinies, bears punishment, and performs a great deed, while Mr. Carlton wins a wager.

Like Bassett's stories of lumber, wool, leather, and glass, the book teaches an industry through adventure, with thanks to the American Sugar Refining Company and Senator Truman G. Palmer. Chapters end with a new year dawning, after lessons in work, fairness, and pluck.
7826-l-p-m-the-end-of-the-great-war:
J. Stewart Barney's L. P. M., The End of the Great War, published in 1915, imagines one man with a secret that could stop the fighting. Chapters run from the man and the hour, a one-man secret, and crossing with royalty through rebuffs, echoes from the Wilhelmstrasse, and a rusty cannon ball.

Diplomacy wins, a spy-driven taxi follows, Buckingham Palace opens, the hero meets the king, and a deionizer shows force. Later come a royal tea table, soldiers all around, a dinner at the Britz, and a voice in the telephone. It is a bold wartime fantasy of invention ending war.
793-aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war:
Frederick A. Talbot wrote this account of flying machines in war, at a time when their use was still new and much debated. He traces the dirigible balloon and the aeroplane from early trials to their first service, weighing what each could do for scouting, bombing, and naval work. Theories, he notes, outran proof for years.

Talbot gathers reports from the first air war, with details on types, crews, and raids. His prose is clear and factual, aimed at readers who want to grasp a fast-changing art. The book is a valuable record of how war in the air looked while it was still being invented, before later histories tidied the story.
8101-bertram-cope-s-year:
Henry Blake Fuller followed a year in the life of Bertram Cope, a young man at a college tea. Through Sunday calls, dinners, excursions, a house party, sailing, cross-purposes, and a distressful Christmas. The chapter headings trace Cope under scrutiny, considered and considered further, entertained by several ladies, committed, rescued, and in danger anew. The setting is university and small-town society, where reputation is watched closely.

Fuller's novel is a comedy of manners with a serious undercurrent, about a young instructor navigating admirers, patrons, and his own uncertain desires. Published in an era that could not name its subject plainly, it has since been recognised as an early American novel of same-sex affection. It remains a subtle, witty portrait of social life and private feeling.
8222-early-letters-of-george-wm-curtis-t:
George Willis Cooke edited these early letters of George William Curtis to John S. Dwight, covering Brook Farm and Concord. Curtis was born in Providence on February 24, 1824, schooled at Jamaica Plain and Providence, and inseparable from his brother Burrill. About 1835 he came under Ralph Waldo Emerson's influence, hearing him in Providence, and the letters that follow show a young man entering the Transcendentalist circle at Brook Farm and Concord.

The letters are fresh, idealistic, and observant, recording communal experiments, conversations, and the hopes of youth. They give a ground-level view of Brook Farm from inside, by a participant who later became a famous editor and reformer. For students of American Transcendentalism, the volume is a delightful primary source.
8385-the-short-line-war:
Samuel Merwin's novel turns on a railroad war, with Jim Weeks at its center and a struggle for possession of a short line. Chapters move through Tillman City politics, judges Black and Grey, and a matter of possession. Later chapters bring somebody losing the books, a politician, Katherine, train number 14, and a capture at Brushingham. Rival interests fight for control of the line throughout.

Merwin, writing in the age of railroad trusts, uses the short line as a picture of American business and politics: courts, promoters, and townsfolk all pulled into the fight. The novel reads as both adventure and commentary on how railroads shaped towns. Readers of business fiction will find a brisk, plot-driven tale from the railroad era.
8440-men-in-war:
Andreas Latzko wrote Men in War from the Austro-Hungarian side of the First World War. Its contents tell the arc: Off to War, Baptism of Fire, The Victor, My Comrade, A Hero's Death, and Home Again. The opening story sets a war hospital garden in late autumn of the war's second year, where soldiers wait between battles.

Latzko, himself an officer wounded in the war, writes against glorification, showing fear, friendship, and the gap between home and front. Dedicated to friend and foe, the book was banned in some countries for its pacifist force. Readers get short, intense stories that rank among the war's most humane fiction, unsparing and compassionate at once.
8576-by-sheer-pluck-a-tale-of-the-ashant:
G. A. Henty tells this boys' adventure through Frank Hargate, a schoolboy first seen fishing and watching a chaffinch nest threatened by a snake. School rivalries, house matches, and country walks fill the opening, before Frank's courage and quick thinking carry him toward West Africa and the Ashanti War. Henty builds his hero the usual way: decent, observant, and steady when danger arrives.

The war chapters put Frank among soldiers, marches, and fighting in unfamiliar country, where pluck, in Henty's phrase, matters more than polish. The book belongs to the late Victorian school of empire adventure, written to stir and instruct young readers at once. Modern readers will notice its period attitudes, but its pace, clear action, and school-to-battlefield arc explain why Henty stayed popular with boys for decades.
92-tarzan-and-the-jewels-of-opar:
Gold from the lost city of Opar draws Tarzan back to its vaults, and trouble follows. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar opens with Belgian and Arab rivals on the road to the city. The priestess La still guards the altar of the Flaming God.

Tarzan steals jewels, loses his reason, and leads the apes again as a beast. Werper the Belgian steals the treasure in turn, and Jane Clayton faces capture and peril. The novel weaves two thefts and a rescue into one chase. Opar's gold keeps pulling Tarzan between man and ape.
9542-graded-poetry-seventh-year:
Katherine D. Blake and Georgia Alexander edited Graded Poetry: Seventh Year in 1906, a school reader of verse for young pupils. The book splits the year in halves, moving from Shakespeare and Milton through Burns, Wordsworth, Scott, and Byron. Poems include The Star-Spangled Banner, Lochinvar, John Gilpin, and The Solitary Reaper. Each piece was picked to suit a child's ear and mind.

First-half poems stress good name, noble nature, and brave deeds, while later poems widen to nature, war, and home. Notes and order guide a teacher through the school year. A reader gets a fine old school anthology, and a view of what American children once learned by heart.
9617-echoes-of-the-war:
J. M. Barrie, famed for Peter Pan, wrote Echoes of the War in 1918, four short plays of wartime London. The Old Lady Shows Her Medals opens, as three charwomen and a hostess talk war over tea. The New Word, Barbara's Wedding, and A Well-Remembered Voice complete the set. Barrie's people are plain folk, and his war is felt at home, not on the front.

Medals, weddings, and remembered voices carry grief, pride, and hope in small rooms. Barrie's humor stays gentle, even as loss shadows each play. A reader gets a tender, humane view of war's home front, from a master of sentiment who knew how to make small scenes ache.
9868-the-united-states-since-the-civil-w:
Charles Ramsdell Lingley, Dartmouth history professor, wrote The United States Since the Civil War in 1920, a survey from Reconstruction to the World War. Chapters follow Grant's time, the new era's economic roots, and the politics of the early eighties. The overturn of 1884, transportation, industry, and laissez faire follow, with diplomacy, wage earners, and money problems.

Later chapters treat 1896, war with Spain, imperialism, Roosevelt, and Wilson, closing with America and the World War. Maps and an index aid study. A reader gets a clear, compact national history, fit for students of modern America.
9944-the-conquest-of-fear:
Basil King's book, with a new introduction by Henry C. Link, argues that fear, not circumstance, rules most unhappy lives. King, writing from his own experience, traces fear from a life-principle through ideas about God, the mind of today, and the world as it is.

Later chapters name the false god of fear, face the fear of death, and point toward abundance of life. The tone is personal and earnest, closer to a friend's counsel than a lecture. Readers looking for early twentieth-century spiritual self-help will find a sincere, plainspoken attempt to answer worry with faith.
a-short-history-of-the-great-war:
A. F. Pollard, professor of English history in the University of London, published A Short History of the Great War in 1920, as the title page records. In twenty chapters with nineteen maps he tells the whole First World War in one volume, from the breach of the peace to the foundations of the peace settlement.

The narrative follows the German invasion, the making of the Western Front, the failure of offensives, and the defeat of Russia. Sea war, the Balkans, and political reactions at home get their own chapters before the tide turns in 1918. Pollard writes as a professional historian close to the events, and the book served a generation that wanted the war explained whole.
aeroplanes-and-dirigibles-of-war:
Frederick A. Talbot explains, in plain language, how aircraft were being used in the great war then raging in Europe. His preface says the book draws on official reports and men who took part, from British, French, Russian, and German sources. Captive balloons, airships, and aeroplanes all get full treatment.

Chapters cover Germany's airship fleet, scouting from the skies, guiding artillery fire, dropping bombs, armored planes, fights in the air, and guns built to shoot aircraft down. Later chapters take up wireless, naval use, and fleets of the air. The book shows how fast flight changed war while the change was still new.
an-art-lovers-guide-to-the-exposition-ex:
Sheldon Cheney wrote An Art-Lover's Guide to the Exposition as a handbook to the art of the San Francisco exposition, printed at Berkeley in 1915 as its title page shows. He promises two things: to explain the symbolism of the architecture, sculpture, and mural painting, and to point out the special qualities that give each work its appeal.

Chapters walk the grounds court by court — Abundance, the Universe, the Four Seasons, Palms and Flowers. Then take up the Tower of Jewels, the machine and fine arts palaces, and the outdoor sculpture. A closing section guides study inside the fine arts galleries themselves. For a visitor then, or a reader now, it preserves how the fair's art was meant to be read.
ballads-of-peace-in-war:
Michael Earls gathered his verse in Ballads of Peace in War, a book of poems shaped by the First World War and by older American wars. Earls, a Jesuit priest and teacher, writes in ballad stanzas meant to be read aloud. His first poem watches a woman keeping vigil for a sailor at sea. Love and prayer, in his telling, guard the absent man.

Other ballads retell brave deeds and narrow escapes. One poem follows a rider sent to fetch the countersign before a Civil War regiment can advance toward Manassas. Soldiers, mothers, and sweethearts share the pages. Earls favors clear stories, strong rhythm, and Catholic faith over modern experiment. Readers find wartime verse that seeks consolation and courage rather than bitterness about the fighting.
bleek-comparative-grammar:
Wilhelm Bleek published his Comparative Grammar of South African Languages in 1862. The German scholar worked in Cape Town among speakers of many tongues. His book founded the true study of the Bantu language family.

Bleek showed that the Bantu tongues form one great linked family. He worked out their sound laws as Grimm had for Europe's tongues. Noun classes and shared roots lock his case into firm order. The feat ranks among the age's great wins in language science. Scholars still cite his Cape Town work as the field's true start point. Bleek gave African tongues the same respect long given to Europe's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abiathar:
Abiathar was a high priest descended through Achimelech, Achitob, Phinees, Heli, and Ithamar from Aaron, whose name means father of plenty. He alone escaped the slaughter at Nob, fled to David during his banishment, and advised him through his campaigns. With the high priest Sadoc he helped carry the ark to Jerusalem, and he stayed close to David in flight, giving counsel at key moments.

His fortunes turned when he backed Adonias for the throne. Solomon's banishment of him to Anathoth finished the ruin of Ithamar's house foretold in Samuel. The entry tracks his career passage by passage through Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, and points readers to commentaries for the puzzle of 2 Samuel 8:17.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adar:
Adar is four things at once, and this entry separates them. First, a frontier town in Chanaan's south, named in Numbers 34:4 and Joshua 15:3, which has not been identified. Second, it is a king of Edom in Genesis 36:39, called Adad, or Hadad in the Revised Version, at 1 Chronicles 1:50.

Third, Adar is the twelfth month of the Jewish year, matching roughly late February to mid-March. Fourth, Adar is a Chaldean god, whose name appears in the compound Adramelech, meaning Adar is King (2 Kings 17:31). The short entry thus serves as a sorting of one name across place, person, calendar, and god.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-anton-:
Albert Anton von Muchar was an Austrian historian born at Linz in Tyrol in 1781 and dead at Graz in 1849. Descended from the old noble Muchar family, he studied at Graz and joined the Benedictine order at Admont. He was ordained a priest soon after taking his vows in 1808. He later became librarian and keeper of the archives at his monastery, then professor of Greek and eastern languages there.

Muchar's tastes ran to history rather than pure language study. His historical works rest on close reading of original sources in libraries across Austria, Bavaria, and northern Italy. Vienna's Academy of Sciences elected him a member in 1829, and he helped found the Historical Society for Inner Austria. His chief works include Roman Noricum in two volumes and his nine-volume History of the Duchy of Styria, the first four volumes edited by himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avatar:
Avatar comes from the Sanskrit avatara, meaning descent, and names a god's descent to earth in Hindu religion. A portion of the god's essence then takes a coarser form, animal, monster, or man. Vishnu's descents matter most, falling in different ages and measures of his essence. Their number runs from ten to twenty-eight, at last countless.

Any man may be hailed as a more or less perfect avatar of Vishnu. The entry counts that homage to men, above all to sect founders, among Hinduism's worst features. The ten most famous avatars open with the Fish, which saved Manu from the Deluge. Next come the Tortoise, bearing Mount Mandara in the churning of the ocean of milk, and the Boar, lifting the earth from flood. Later avatars adopt the cults of Rama, Krsna, and Buddha, yet their likeness to the Incarnation is most superficial.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldachium-of:
A baldachium is a dome-like canopy over the high altar of larger churches. It usually stands on four columns, though sometimes it hangs by chains from the roof. Its late medieval name, baldacchino, comes from Baghdad, source of the precious cloths for such canopies. Earlier it was called ciborium, from Greek kiborion, the lotus seed-pod used as a drinking cup.

It likely arose from the wish to give the plain altar table a dignified architectural setting. By the fourth century it formed the church's architectural center, marking the altar as a throne of honor. Altar curtains hung between its columns, and lamps and crowns hung from its roof. Use ran general until the twelfth century, when the reliquary displaced it, though Italy kept the older form. The most magnificent baldachium is Bernini's in St Peter's, Rome, made for Urban VIII.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baltasar:
Baltasar is the Greek and Latin form of Belshazzar, Hebrew Bel-sarra-usur, meaning 'May Bel protect the king.' Bel was Babylon's chief and titular god. In Daniel chapter five, Baltasar appears as son of Nabuchodonosor and last King of Babylon. While he feasted his nobles, the Medes under Darius invaded the town, and the king was slain.

At the feast he defiled vessels taken from Jerusalem, and his wives and concubines drank from them. A hand then wrote Mane, Thecel, Phares on the wall, which no counsellor or magician could explain. The Queen urged calling Daniel, who read the doom: the kingdom was numbered, the king weighed and found wanting. Its rule would pass to the Medes and the Persians. Herodotus names Labynitus II as Babylon's last king, commonly read as a corruption of Nabonidus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boso-breakspe:
Boso Breakspear, third English cardinal, rose as nephew of Adrian IV and steered the papacy through the schism of 1159. A Benedictine of Saint Albans famed for piety and learning, he wrote lives of eleventh- and twelfth-century popes, including his uncle, and versified saints' lives now in the Cotton manuscripts. Adrian made him cardinal-deacon in December 1155 and camerlengo, and sent him to Portugal.

On Adrian's death, four imperial cardinals chose Octavian as Victor IV, but Boso led twenty-three cardinals into Sant'Angelo on burial day, 5 September 1159, and elected Rolando as Alexander III. Alexander raised him to cardinal-priest in 1163 and took him to Venice for the Peace of 1177 with Frederick. Boso died at Rome about 1181.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buenaventura-:
Buenaventura Sitjar, a Majorcan Franciscan, spent his life at California's San Antonio mission and preserved its Telame language. Born at Porrera, Majorca, on 9 December 1739, he took the habit of Saint Francis in April 1758 and joined the College of San Fernando in Mexico after ordination. Assigned to California in 1770, he landed at San Diego on 21 May 1771.

Present at San Antonio's founding, he served as its first missionary under Junipero Serra until his death on 3 September 1808. By then 3,400 Indians had been baptized there. He mastered Telame, the mission's tongue, and put together a vocabulary with Spanish explanations, issued at New York in 1861. Shorter than Arroyo's Mutsun dictionary, his work gives pronunciation and fuller notes, and he also left a journal of a 1795 exploring expedition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bye-altar: A bye-altar is an altar that ranks below the central or high altar of a church. The name is most often given to altars set in the bays of the nave, the transepts, or other side spaces. Such altars stand apart from the high altar yet within the same church, giving each bay or transept its own place of worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canons-and-ca:
Canons regular are religious clerics who live under a rule while serving the Church's sacramental and pastoral work. The entry sets them apart from monks, for whom clerical status is incidental rather than essential. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, it argues that their order exists precisely for work tied to the divine mysteries. Erasmus himself, a canon regular, called it a middle path between monastic life and the secular clergy.

From origins in the early Church the entry follows their growth, reforms, and congregations across the centuries. It contrasts their choral duties, discipline, dress, and diet with those of Benedictines and Cistercians. English houses get close attention, with dozens founded between the Conquest and the death of Henry II. The account closes with the canonesses regular, the women's branch of the same life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cardinal-vica:
The cardinal vicar is the pope's vicar-general for the spiritual government of Rome and its surrounding district, properly called Vicarius Urbis. The entry opens with a critical list of vicars from 1100 to 1600, built from earlier lists by Ponzetti, Moroni, Crostarosa, and Eubel with new manuscript finds. Names before 1100, it warns, must count as uncertain, with Bovo of Tusculum about 1106 the first clearly attested holder.

Until 1260 vicars came from the cardinals, and the first drawn from nearby bishops followed after that date. Later sections set out nomination and oath, authority, the vicegerent, and the organization of the vicariate. Departments covered include ordinations, religious orders, preaching, parochial clergy, the court, and the secretariate. A reform by Pius X, published after the entry's main source, gets a closing note.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-cal:
A vast entry on the Christian calendar, the Church's reckoning of time and feasts. It opens with the calendars of Egypt, Babylon, China, India, and the Aztecs, the Celtic calendar stones found at Coligny in 1897, and the verse Fasti of Ovid. It then turns to the Jewish calendar of Leviticus, with lunar months of 29 and 30 days corrected to keep pace with the moon and the sun.

The main body covers the Easter cycle, the Nativity, and saints' days. It goes on to the earliest calendars and feasts of Our Lady and the apostles. Later developments and the modern calendar imposed by authority follow, ending with the churches of the East. Greek movable feasts get close attention, from Sexagesima, the Sunday of abstinence from flesh, to All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost, our Trinity Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerks-regula:
Clerks regular join the religious state's perfection to the priestly office. Essentially clerics, they devote themselves to preaching, sacraments, education of youth, and works of mercy. At the same time they are religious in the strictest sense, professing solemn vows and living community life under a rule approved by the sovereign pontiff. Canon law often uses the term for canons regular, and authors class regular clerks as a branch of the regular canons.

They serve primarily the sacred ministry, not contemplation. They must cultivate the sacred sciences, which monks are not bound to by state of life. As clerics they keep clerical dress distinct from monk's habit and cowl. Their occupations leave them less given to austerity. They differ from friars in being primarily priests, and from canons regular in holding no cathedral churches and giving themselves more to ministry than to choir service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diakovar:
A place and diocesan entry on Diakovar in Slavonia, seat of the united dioceses of Bosnia and Syrmia. In 1900 its 6,824 people were mostly Catholic, about two-thirds Serb and over a quarter German. A Romanesque-Gothic cathedral, finished in 1883 from Rösner's plans by Friedrich Schmidt, runs 256 feet long. Twin towers rise near 276 feet, with a cupola near 203 feet, Seitz frescoes, and an organ of 3,000 pipes.

Roman roots show in the Certissa station on the road from Sissek to Sirmium, lost when peoples moved across Europe in the fourth and fifth centuries. A thirteenth-century gift of Possessio Diaco to the Bishop of Bosnia revived the site, and the see moved to Diakovar in 1246. Seminary, Sisters of Charity house, and episcopal palace complete the picture, with Mariaschnee as the diocese's famed pilgrimage place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dithmar:
Dithmar, also called Thietmar, was bishop of Merseburg and a medieval chronicler. He was born on 25 July 975, son of Count Siegfried of Walbeck and kin to the Saxon emperors. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his schooling at Quedlinburg, Bergen, and Magdeburg. He became provost of Walbeck in 1002, priest in 1003, and fourth bishop of Merseburg in 1009.

As bishop he labored to restore a diocese nearly ruined by his predecessor Giseler, who had chased the archbishopric of Magdeburg. He also defended the freedom of church elections against grasping princes. His chronicle, the great work of his life, remains a chief source for the Saxon age, and the entry lists the editions through which it has reached modern readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingo-de-sa:
Domingo de Salazar was born at La Bastida on the Ebro in 1512 and died at Madrid in 1594. He joined the Dominicans at San Esteban in Salamanca and was sent to Mexico, where he took a master's degree in theology and a professor's chair. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his wish to preach to the heathen was granted in the province of Guajaca, where he defended Indian rights with zeal.

From Mexico he passed to Florida, laboring for years in toil and privation, then back to Mexico as prior and vice-provincial. After forty years of mission life he was sent to Madrid on order business. The entry closes with his tomb's Latin praise, calling him a father to the poor and poor himself, a fitting epitaph for a defender of the Indians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-double-altar: A double altar carries a double front, allowing Mass to be said on both sides of it at once. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that such altars are often found in churches of religious communities where the choir stands behind the altar. One priest may offer the Holy Sacrifice for the choir community while another offers it for the laity in the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eleazar:
Eleazar is the name of several men in the Bible. This entry starts with the greatest. Eleazar son of Aaron succeeded his father as high priest, wearing Aaron's robes after his death. He stood beside Moses in counting Israel. He helped settle the inheritance claim of the daughters of Salphaad. He shared out the spoils from the Madianites. He heard the plea of Ruben and Gad for land east of the Jordan.

Moses himself presented Joshua, his successor, to Eleazar. Eleazar headed the list of those who divided the land west of the Jordan. He was buried at Gabaath in Mount Ephraim, on ground given to his son Phinees. Down to the Maccabees, the high priests came from his line, apart from the years from Heli to Solomon. The entry also tells of Eleazar Abaron, son of Mathathias, crushed beneath an elephant he had stabbed at Bethzacharam.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friar:
Friar names a member of a mendicant order, a begging brotherhood that lives by ministry rather than by cloistered retreat. The word comes from the Latin frater, through French and Middle English forms, and by the late thirteenth century it marked the new orders in English writing. The entry draws the line between friar and monk with care.

For the monk, solitude stands first, and his order may hold property in common. For the friar, public ministry is the heart of life, and his vow of poverty once barred even corporate ownership, so friars lived on free gifts. The Council of Trent later let most mendicant orders hold property together, the Friars Minor and Capuchins alone excepted. Jesuits, though mendicant in spirit, count as clerks regular instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gibraltar:
Gibraltar is a rugged promontory in Andalusia, about six miles round, whose rock rises to 1,396 feet above the strait. The ancient Mount Calpe, paired with Abyla across the water as the Pillars of Hercules, it passed from Phoenicians and Romans to Visigoths and Moors. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces its sieges and its passage from Spain to Britain.

Tarik's Moors built a castle on the rock in 711 and gave it the name Gibel-Tarik, whence Gibraltar. After eight sieges the Spaniards retook it in 1462. In 1704 an English and Dutch force took it during the War of the Spanish Succession. The Treaty of Utrecht made it British in 1713. Its fourteenth and last siege ran from July 1779 for three years, seven months, and twelve days, and failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamar:
Norway's medieval diocese of Hamar covered Hedemarken and Christians Amt, formed in 1152 from Oslo when Arnold, former Bishop of Gardar in Greenland, became its first bishop. He began Christ Church cathedral, finished about the time of Bishop Paul in the mid-thirteenth century. The see grew a chapter of ten canons, a school, a Dominican priory, and a monastery.

Later bishops include Thorfinn, exiled to Flanders where he died, Jörund, moved to Trondhjem, and a provincial council held in 1380. Mogens, the last Catholic bishop, ruled from 1513 to 1537 before a Danish noble seized him in his castle and carried him to Antvorskov. There he lived mildly treated until his death in 1542.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-frie:
Henry of Friemar, a German theologian born at Friemar near Gotha toward the end of the thirteenth century, entered the Augustinian Hermits young and was posted to the University of Paris. There he became master of sacred theology and taught until 1318. That year he became regent of studies at St. Thomas's monastery in Prague and examiner for Germany, later provincial for Thuringia and Saxony. He probably died at Erfurt about 1355.

His printed works show wide range. They include a collection of sermons on the saints, a treatise on the fourfold instinct, divine, angelic, diabolic, and human, and additions to the Sentences. A work on spirits and their discernment, a tract on the conception of the Blessed Virgin, and a history of the origins of the Augustinian Hermits complete the list. His writings circulated in print from Cologne to Parma and Louvain across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-kalk:
Henry of Kalkar, a Carthusian writer born at Kalkar in Cleves in 1328, studied at Cologne and Paris. He became Master of Arts in 1357, procurator of the German nation, and professor of theology. After canonries at Kaiserswerth and Cologne he withdrew in 1365 to Cologne's Charterhouse. He rose to prior of Arnheim, Ruremonde, Cologne, and Strasburg, and served twenty years as visitor amid the Great Schism. Relieved of office in 1396, he lived in prayer at Cologne until his death in 1408.

Kalkar was celebrated as reformer as well as writer: at Arnheim he drew Gerard Groote into the Charterhouse. His writings influenced the school of Deventer and Windesheim, organizing the Catholic Renaissance that found expression at Trent. Many wrongly credited him with the Rosary and the Imitation, yet the Exercitatorium Monachale is certainly his, inspiring Thomas à Kempis and supplying ideas for Ignatius's Exercises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-fr:
Two German works on mysticism carry the name Hermann of Fritzlar, and this entry sorts out what belongs to him and what does not. The first, Das Heiligenleben, is a set of ninety-one short sermons on saints' lives written between 1343 and 1349. It mixes plain teaching with mystical thought on union with God and the birth of Christ in the soul. Long credited to Hermann, it was in fact compiled at his request by the Dominican preacher Gisiler of Slatheim.

The second work, Blume der Schauung, or Flower of Contemplation, survives in a Nuremberg manuscript. It gathers loosely linked questions on the contemplative life and its models. Readers interested in fourteenth-century German mysticism find here a careful untangling of authorship, sources, and the blend of first- and third-person voice in the sermons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-high-altar:
The high altar is the chief altar in a church, raised on an elevated plane in the sanctuary so that all the faithful can see it at once. It symbolizes Christ, and it serves as the banquet table on which Christ offers himself through the priest's hands to the Eternal Father. A sacrifice supposes both priest and altar, and the Acts of the Apostles shows the faithful sharing in the prayers and partaking of the victim.

In early days the altar usually stood in a chapel at the head of the church, facing east, following the tradition that the faithful pray toward the east. If a church could not be built that way, the altar stood opposite the chief doorway. Olden churches had but one altar, and the entry traces how the high altar's place, form, and meaning developed from those beginnings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-th:
The Christian altar is an elevated, table-like surface for offering the Sacrifice of the Mass. Its earliest scriptural reference is in St. Paul, who sets the table of the Lord, trapeza Kyriou, against the table of devils, or pagan altars. Greek Fathers kept trapeza as their favourite term, while Hebrews calls the altar thysiasterion, a word used by Ignatius and later Fathers for the Christian altar.

Christians of the first age carefully avoided bomos, with its pagan associations, until Synesius used it in the early fifth century. Latin writers used altare, mensa, ara, and altarium, though ara more often meant a pagan altar. The entry traces names, forms, and fittings from those early tables through great church altars, their columns, and the iconostasis of the Greek church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-issachar:
Issachar names both a man and a tribe, and this entry sorts the two. First, he was the ninth son of Jacob and fifth son of Leah. He was named for a circumstance of his birth. Scripture tells little of him beyond his four sons at the descent into Egypt. Second, the tribe descended from him, about which knowledge stays thin. In the wilderness march the tribe camped east of the tabernacle with Judah and Zebulun.

At Sinai's first census Issachar counted 54,400 warriors, and 64,300 at the second census, figures the entry quotes from Numbers. After entering western Palestine the tribe settled its allotted land, its later story fading from the record. Readers get a careful distinction: a patriarch known mainly as a name, and a tribe known mainly through census rolls and camp order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-goar:
Dominican and Hellenist Jacques Goar was born at Paris in 1601. He died on 23 September 1653. He entered the Annunciation convent in Rue St Honoré in 1619. He professed there on 24 May 1620. Though lector of philosophy and theology, he devoted himself to Greek study. His superiors sent him to the East to serve Rome through knowledge of Greek church documents and positive theology.

He lived at Chios as missionary apostolic and prior of St Sebastian convent. He used travel to observe rites, meet Orthodox scholars, and study Catholic-Orthodox points at issue. About 1640 he returned to Rome bearing many manuscripts, some valuable. Thereafter he corresponded with the most learned Greeks of his day. The entry presents a scholar-diplomat bridging Latin and Greek Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jewish-calend:
The Jewish Calendar entry explains how Israel has reckoned time from earliest days to the present. The day runs sunset to sunset, or to the first three stars, and before exile daylight was split only into morning, midday, and evening. Babylon brought twelve varying hours, the first near six in the morning and the sixth ending at noon.

Nights were first kept in three watches, to midnight, to cock-crow near three, and to dawn. Weeks count seven numbered days, the seventh called Sabbath, a name also used for the week itself, while Friday bears the title eve of Sabbath or day of preparation. Months, feasts, and leap years complete a system binding worship to seasons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomucene Brischar was a German church historian who spent his working life as a parish priest. Born at Horb in Wurttemberg in 1819, he studied theology at Tubingen and served from 1853 until his death in 1897 as parish priest of Buhl near Rottenburg.

His chief task was continuing Count Leopold Stolberg's History of the Religion of Jesus Christ. He wrote its forty-fifth through fifty-fourth volumes. The entry judges that work below his predecessor's standard. He also wrote two volumes on the disputes between Paolo Sarpi and Pallavicini. He added a monograph on Pope Innocent III, a five-volume survey of Catholic pulpit orators in Germany, and many articles for Herder's church lexicon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ludwig:
Joseph Ludwig Colmar was the Bishop of Mainz who rebuilt its church life after the Revolution. Born at Strasbourg in 1760 and ordained in 1783, he stayed in the city through the Terror in disguise, giving the sacraments in secret. After Robespierre's fall he preached across Strasbourg, and Napoleon named him Bishop of Mainz in 1802.

Colmar found his cathedral profaned and his diocese ruined by war and confiscation. He rebuilt and reconsecrated the cathedral, saved Speyer's from demolition, opened a seminary in 1804, and visited every parish and school. During the epidemic of 1813 and 1814 he served the sick himself. He died at Mainz in 1818.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-of-iss: Joseph of Issachar is a figure known from a single verse of the Bible. A man of the tribe of Issachar, he was the father of Igal, one of the twelve spies Moses sent to scout Canaan. Their task was to report on the land and its people. The entry, citing Numbers 13:8, gives no further detail about his life, deeds, or death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madagascar:
Madagascar is the great island south-east of Africa, sighted 10 August 1500 by Diego Dias, parted from Cabral's fleet of thirteen ships out of Lisbon, and named St. Lawrence for the martyr's feast day. It stretches from about 12 to 26 degrees south, with St. Mary, Mayotte, and Nossi-Be nearby.

Sparsely settled, barely thirteen souls to the square mile, dense in the centre and thin elsewhere, its peoples now sit under a French governor-general at Tananarivo. They include Hova, Betsileo, Sakalava, and Betsimisaraka. Grandidier and most anthropologists trace them to the black Indonesian race of the Malayo-Polynesian world. Their agglutinative tongue, Malagasy, is rich in material speech and poor in abstractions, and their religion blends a mixed monotheism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malabar:
Malabar, in its narrow sense, was a district of India down the west coast south of Mangalore. It ran about 145 miles, in the region of present-day Kerala. Its chief towns were Cannanore, Tellicherry, Calicut, and Palghat. Its old name, Male, meant where the pepper grows, and it gave Malayalam its name.

Widely used, Malabar Coast meant the whole south-west corner of India back to the ghats. In church terms, British Malabar fell under Mangalore. Cochin state held the Padroado diocese of Cochin, the Archdiocese of Verapoly, and three vicariates. Travancore lay under Quilon. Syrian Christians of Malabar lived chiefly in those three vicariates. The famed Malabar Rites, oddly, had nothing to do with Malabar itself. Their scene was Madura, across the peninsula.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mechitar:
Mechitar, a name meaning Comforter, was taken by Peter Manuk of Sebaste when he became a monk and founded the Mechitarist order. Born at Sebaste in Lesser Armenia in 1676 to parents of reputed noble blood, he was raised to fifteen by two pious nuns. He entered the cloister of the Holy Cross near Sebaste and was ordained deacon in 1691. Thirst for learning soon drew him out toward Etchmiadzin.

On the road he met a European missionary and an Armenian whose tales of Western wonders changed his life. Fired with love for Western culture, he wandered and taught for scant wages. After eighteen months he returned to Sebaste, still bent on Western study. There he conceived a religious society, perhaps prompted by the suppressed United Brothers, that would wed Armenian faith to Western learning and win his countrymen to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nuestra-senor:
Our Lady of the Pillar, a celebrated shrine at Saragossa in Spain, honors an image of the Virgin set on a marble pillar. The present Baroque church began in 1681, and the image was crowned in 1905 with a crown valued at 450,000 pesetas, a mark of devotion across the kingdom.

Tradition says Saint James built the first shrine at Mary's wish after she appeared by the Ebro, a story Duchesne and Baronius doubt and defenders support from Jerome and the Mozarabic office. Written devotion at Saragossa is traced to Pedro Librana in 1155 and to Roman-era tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portable-alta:
A portable altar is a solid slab of natural stone, hard enough to resist any fracture. A bishop, or another person with faculties, must consecrate it. The slab sits in or on the altar table, about two inches from the front edge. It is raised enough to feel under the cloths.

It must be big enough for the Sacred Host and most of the chalice's base, and for the ciborium too when Communion is given. Five Greek crosses mark it, one at each corner and one at the centre, showing where unctions fall at consecration. If the centre cross is missing, the unction still must not be skipped, though skipping it would not void the consecration. Greeks instead use the antimensium, a consecrated silk or linen cloth like a corporal. It is made by placing cloth on a consecrated altar and pouring wine and chrism over it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-privileged-al:
An altar counts as privileged when each Mass said there also gains a plenary indulgence for the single soul of the Mass's intention. The privileged altar must be fixed. It need not be consecrated, so long as a consecrated stone, a portable altar, sits in its table.

The privilege clings to the structure itself, not its altar stone, by its title. Hence the privilege stands if the altar's stuff is changed, if it moves to another place, or if another altar with the same title takes its place in the same church. It stands even under the altar's desecration or profanation. To win the indulgence, the Mass must be a Requiem Mass when the rubrics allow it. If a feast's higher rite or other cause bars a Requiem, another Mass may win it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-the:
Reform of the calendar begins with nature's units, the day and the year. This encyclopedia entry defines the day as the interval between two passages of the sun across a place's meridian. Civil reckoning counts from the midnight passage, while astronomers count from the following noon. So the civil day runs twelve hours ahead of the astronomical day. The solar day runs about four minutes longer than the sidereal day.

The Julian system drifted, losing about three-quarters of a day per century, or three whole days in four centuries. After Caesar's murder in 44 BC, a misunderstanding made leap year fall every third year instead of every fourth. At the Julian reform the sun passed the spring equinox on 25 March, but by Nicaea in 325 the date had moved to the 21st, then fixed as the proper equinox date. For the Gregorian New Style's spread, the entry points to Chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatical-ye:
The sabbatical year, the seventh year, was devoted to cessation of agriculture, also called the Year of Remission. Three prescriptions were observed: the land lay fallow and all farm labour was suspended, with no plowing, sowing, or tending vines and olives. The spontaneous yield was not garnered but left in fields for common use, and what was unused was abandoned to cattle and wild animals.

The prescribed rest was for the land, not for man, so non-farm work was not forbidden. With no crops reaped, debt payment would have been a hardship. A creditor could not press an Israelite for a debt, though strangers could still be pressed. Commentators dispute whether this meant remission or mere suspension of payment during the year. During the sabbatical year the Law was read at Tabernacles to all Israel and strangers within the gates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-leodega:
Leodegar, bishop of Autun, was born about 615 to the high-ranking Sigrada and Bobilo. He died a martyr in 678 at Sarcing on the Somme. His childhood passed at the court of Clotaire II, and he later studied at Poitiers under his uncle, the bishop there, who ordained him deacon.

He became a priest, withdrew to the monastery of Saint Maxentius in 650, and was soon elected abbot, reforming the community under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Called to court in 656 by Queen Bathildis to help govern and teach her children, he was later named bishop of Autun. There he held a council in 661 that struck at Manichaeism, built three baptisteries, enlarged Saint-Nazaire, and set up a refuge for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scapular:
The scapular, from the Latin scapula, shoulder, forms part, now the chief part, of monastic habits, and many other orders and congregations, male and female, have adopted it. Worn over habit or soutane, it is essentially a cloth band about breast-width, fourteen to eighteen inches across, hanging nearly to the feet front and back. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a garment turned devotion.

A head opening sits in the middle, with narrow bands resting on the shoulders. Older forms joined front and back by cross bands under the arms, making a cross over breast and back. Shorter forms exist for layfolk, and the famous brown scapular of Carmel carries promises for its wearers. The entry traces monastic origins, confraternities, indulgences, and the many coloured scapulars of later devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anschar:
St. Anschar, or Ansgarius, called the Apostle of the North, was born in Picardy on 8 September 801 and died on 5 February 865. This entry follows a Benedictine of Corbie who passed into Westphalia. He then sailed with Harold, the newly baptized and exiled King of Denmark returning home, to preach where Ebbo of Reims had laboured with little success.

Anschar founded a school at Schleswig, but Harold's intemperate zeal provoked a storm ending in a second expulsion, and the missionaries returned. Travelling with Louis the Pious's ambassadors, Anschar then entered Sweden. Though the embassy was attacked and seemingly abandoned, he won the king's leave to preach, planting the faith that would earn him his apostolic title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-goar:
Goar, anchorite of Aquitaine, sought total detachment beside the Rhine and became a pilgrims' host instead. Born about 585 to a distinguished family, he showed sound piety from youth, with prayer filling his heart and meditation his mind. Ordained, he laboured for souls with greater authority, yet longed above all for his own sanctification. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death near Oberwesel to 6 July 649.

About 618 he settled in a lonely place at Trier's edge, near Oberwesel, beside a little chapel he built. There he lived detached from material and perishable things. Fame spread anyway, and pilgrims flocked to him, giving him chances for hospitality and good advice. Two of them denounced him to Rusticus, bishop of Trier, opening a conflict the entry leaves unfolding. Solitude, sought strictly, kept turning into service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ibar:
Ibar, pre-Patrician Irish saint of Wexford, preached before Patrick arrived and then submitted to him. Labouring in present County Wexford from 425 to 450, he recognized Patrick's jurisdiction and was confirmed in his episcopacy, becoming the national apostle's disciple after early reluctance. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 23 April 500, his feast day.

Much obscurity veils his early training, but about 480 he settled at Begerin in Wexford harbour, building an oratory and cell that soon filled with disciples from all Ireland. Aengus's Litany invokes three thousand confessors under his direction. His nephew Abban came to Begerin aged twelve in Ibar's old age and accompanied him to Rome. Patron of Begerin, variously written Ibar, Iberius, and Ivor, he stands as a saint who yielded precedence gracefully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-othmar:
Othmar, first abbot of St Gall, gathered scattered monks into a monastery and died a prisoner for defending its lands. Of Alemannic descent and schooled in Rhaetia, he was ordained priest and led a church of St Florinus. In 720 Waltram of Thurgau set him over the cell of St Gall, where he united its monks under the rule of Columban and became its first abbot.

He built a hospital and a school, and under him the Benedictine rule replaced Columban's. When Counts Warin and Ruodhart tried to seize St Gall's property, Othmar resisted fearlessly. Seized on a journey to Constance, he was held at Bodmann and then on the island of Werd in the Rhine, where he died on 16 November 759 after six months' imprisonment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stripping-of-:
On Holy Thursday evening, after the ciborium is removed, the priest strips the high altar bare. This entry describes that solemn rite step by step. Vested in a violet stole, the celebrant with deacon and subdeacon takes away cloths, flowers, and ornaments. Meanwhile the antiphon Diviserunt sibi and Psalm 21 are recited, leaving only cross and unlit candles.

Every other altar in the church is bared the same way. The altar stands for Christ, stripped of his garments before his tormentors. The bare church marks the pause in the Holy Sacrifice. An older custom of washing altars with hyssop dipped in wine and water, recalled by Isidore and Eligius, closes the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-szatmar:
Szatmar is a Hungarian diocese, suffragan of Eger, formed by King Francis I at the same time as Kassa. It covers Szatmár, Bereg, Mármaros, Ugocsa, and Ungvar counties, with a small part of Szabolcs. Its first bishop, Stephen Fischer, served from 1804 to 1807 before becoming Archbishop of Eger, and successors Klobusiczky and Hám shaped its organization and schools.

Under Hám, who served from 1827 to 1857, the cathedral was enlarged, new churches rose, and many charities were founded; his beatification is under consideration. The present bishop, Tiburtius Boromisza, appointed in 1906, lives at Szatmár-Németi. Five archdeaneries hold 95 parishes with 177 clergy, fifteen monasteries count 703 members, and Roman Catholics number 149,807 against 625,627 Greek Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thangmar:
Thangmar, or Thankmar, was a historian born about the middle of the tenth century and probably died at Hildesheim after 1022. He first appears as head of Hildesheim's cathedral school, later dean, notary, and librarian. Distinguished as scholar and statesman, he taught Bishops Bernward, Meinwerk, and Benno, as well as Emperor Henry II. He wielded great influence over Bernward, directing much episcopal business.

In 1000 he accompanied Bernward to Rome and was sent repeatedly to the imperial court as the bishop's representative, highly esteemed by Otto III. After Bernward's death in 1022 he wrote the bishop's life, gathering material earlier and probably drafting ten chapters in 1008 to 1013. An eyewitness of many events and actor in all important measures, he wrote a plain, simple, unrhetorical, and truthful narrative. Only on the Gandersheim jurisdiction dispute does he seem partisan for Bernward. His Vita Bernwardi ranks among the finest medieval biographies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-knights-t:
Military orders begin with the Templars, their model and their tragedy, and this entry marks their story in three beats: humble beginning, marvellous growth, tragic end. After Jerusalem's deliverance, crusaders went home, leaving a precarious conquest ringed by Muslim neighbours. In 1118 Hugues de Payens and eight companions vowed before Jerusalem's patriarch to defend the Christian kingdom.

Baldwin II housed them beside the Temple, hence Poor Knights of the Temple, living on alms and escorting pilgrims. Donations, banking, and castles followed, until wealth and pride drew Philip IV's prosecution and Clement V's suppression. Trial, torture, and burning close a tale that still grips the imagination.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-legend-of:
Letters exchanged between Christ and a king of Edessa form the legend examined here, recorded by Eusebius in his Church History with firm belief. Three documents carry it: Abgar's letter to the Lord, the Lord's answer, and a portrait painted from life. Eusebius thought the Syriac originals lay in Edessa's archives in his own day.

Medieval East and West loved the tale. Copies of the Lord's letter on parchment, marble, and metal served as talismans and amulets. Syriac text, Armenian translation, two shorter Greek versions, and stone inscriptions survive, and the entry weighs their relations. It is a case study in how a pious story travelled and hardened into relic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-thirty-ye:
Germany's war of 1618 to 1648, pre-eminently German yet European in reach, is the vast conflict surveyed here. Nearly every western European country took part, and its links to other wars of the era and its final results shaped the continent. Fundamental cause lay in imperial decay from 1555: weak imperial power, estates lacking patriotism, and paralysed authority among Protestant estates of the southwest.

Unrest spread through Germany, inviting Spain and the Netherlands to seize footing on the Lower Rhine during the twelve years' truce. Bohemian revolt, Danish, Swedish, and French phases, Wallenstein and Gustavus, and the Peace of Westphalia follow. Devastation, religion, and the new balance of states close one of history's longest wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-marina-de:
Marina de Escobar was a mystic and foundress of a modified branch of the Brigittine Order, born at Valladolid in Spain on 8 February 1554, who died there on 9 June 1633. Her father Iago de Escobar taught civil and canon law and served a time as governor of Osuna, a man famed for learning and saintly life. Her mother Margaret Montana was daughter to Charles V's physician. Marina was an apt scholar, reflective beyond her years even in youth.

Until her forty-fifth year she attended mainly to her own perfection, then she gave herself more to fostering others' piety. At fifty her continual bodily afflictions grew so severe that she stayed bedridden for the rest of her life. Providence gave her an admirable guide in Luis de Ponte. The entry follows her visions, her writings, and the Brigittine reform she inspired.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-joh:
John Sugar, or Suker, was a Staffordshire priest executed at Warwick in July 1604. Born at Wombourn in 1558, he entered Oxford from St Mary Hall in 1584, left without a degree, reportedly because he disliked the Oath of Supremacy. For a time served as a Protestant minister at Cannock.

Ordained from Douai in 1601, he was sent to England the same year. Arrested at Rowington in July 1603 with Robert Greswold, who attended him, Sugar spent a year in Warwick prison. Both were condemned there in July 1604, Sugar as a priest and Greswold as his helper. Sugar was cut down while still living, while Greswold was offered his life if he would promise to conform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicar:
Vicar, from Latin vicarius, one acting instead of another, is explained here as a canon-law term for the representative of a person holding ordinary church jurisdiction. Romans used the title for officials under the praetorian prefects, and the early Church knew vicars of the Apostolic See. Such as the archbishops of Thessalonica, as well as bishops' vicars like archdeacons, archpriests, and rural priests with the cure of souls outside episcopal cities.

In time these offices became part of the Church's ordinary magistracy, treated in Gratian's Decretum and Gregory IX's Decretals, while bishops' vicars-general first appear in later collections. After Trent limited archdeacons, their office nearly vanished, and the council abolished other vicarships incompatible with clerical discipline. A vicar differs from a viceregent, and without special faculties cannot appoint an equal substitute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicar-capitul:
A vicar capitular is the administrator chosen by a cathedral chapter to govern a diocese left vacant by a bishop's death. On the vacancy the canons inherit the episcopal jurisdiction as a body. Within eight days they must meet and constitute a vicar, or the right passes to the metropolitan, the senior suffragan, or the nearest bishop.

Election need not follow a strict form, though votes, if cast, must be secret and no one may vote for himself. The chosen man, ideally a doctor or licentiate in canon law, succeeds to the chapter's whole ordinary jurisdiction. The chapter may neither reserve in part nor take back, and faculties granted to bishops for a term of years pass to him as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-war:
War is defined here in its juridical sense as contention carried on by force of arms between sovereign states, or communities holding the rights of states in that regard. The word is often loosely used for civil strife, sedition, rebellion, or a state's suppression of organized outlaws. The jurist may not so use it, since those struggles lack the juridical standing of war between sovereigns. A people in revolution may, rarely, stand in like juridical case with a state.

Seeking to restore vanished civil government or to vitalize constitutional rights reserved to the people, and protect fundamental rights by arms. Later sections treat belligerency, just title, and necessity: fair opportunity of adjustment, or reasonable assurance that offence will not be rectified except under stress of war. Must precede a just resort to arms, and whether to arbitrate first lies within the aggrieved state's own competence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-dunba:
William Dunbar was a Scottish poet often called the Chaucer of Scotland. Born about 1460, he died about 1520. He took his bachelor's degree at Saint Andrews in 1479, became a Franciscan novice, preached across England, and spent time in Picardy. About 1490 he returned to Scotland and entered the service of James IV, who used him on embassies to Paris and elsewhere and granted him a small pension.

Dunbar marked James's marriage to Margaret of England with The Thrissil and the Rois of 1503, picturing friendship between the two realms as thistle and rose. His other verse includes the Goldyn Targe, an allegory of love beating reason, and a grim Dance of the seven deadly sins, plus humorous and devout pieces. He begged king and queen in vain for a country benefice, and after 1513 no trace of him survives; some guess he fell at Flodden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-seth-:
William Seth Agar was an English canon famed as one of his country's deepest guides in ascetical and mystical theology. Born at York on 25 December 1815, he died on 23 August 1872. Schooled at Prior Park, Bath, he took orders there and was posted to Lyme in Dorset in 1845. Poor health forced him from Lyme twice, and in 1852 he became chaplain to the Augustinian canonesses at Abbotsleigh, where he lived without break until his death.

In 1856 Agar was installed as canon of the Plymouth chapter. Friends called him more a deep thinker than a wide reader, yet he studied many works of theology and philosophy, above all Rosmini, whose writings he annotated with care. His name rests on his grasp of grace at work in souls and on the inner life, a reputation the Tablet marked at his death in September 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zanzibar:
Zanzibar is the East African island and town where Persian and Arab colonists mingled with natives, forming the Swahili people. At a remote unknown period Persians and Arabs settled the coast from Somaliland to Cape Delgado, often called Zanquebar, from Persian Zendj, blacks, and bara, country. Besides Lamu, Malindi, Mombasa, and Kilwa, Zanzibar town became the best-known centre.

Ungudya, the natives' name for the island, spans only 570 square miles for about 100,000 people, over half in the capital. It is famed for clove and coconut plantations held by Arabs and Swahilis, while Hindus, Parsees, Goanese, and Europeans run the town's trade. Bantu natives speak Swahili, kin to equatorial tongues. In old days Zanzibar shipped ivory, copal, skins, grain, and slaves from Bagamoyo and Kilwa across Muslim Indian Ocean lands, sending caravans inland to the Great Lakes. Vasco da Gama took Zanzibar in 1499 and set up an Augustinian convent there.
