fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: FBI interviews from March 2001 collected for the 9/11 Commission. The conspiracy moved toward its terrible climax. These pages preserve those interviews. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.

FBI interviews from March 2002 gathered for the 9/11 Commission. The commission's own probe was in full swing. This file preserves those interviews. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
found-at-blazing-star:
Bret Harte begins this California tale the morning after rain at the mining settlement of Blazing Star. Cass Beard, up early because his cabin roof leaked, crosses the highway and sees something glitter in a red pool. It is not gold quartz but a plain gold ring, and its inscription reads May to Cass, his own nickname, in a camp with no women in it.

Harte lets the find work on a superstitious man. Cass pockets the ring and asks his fellows, too casually, whether anyone lost anything in the night. The answers he gets are jokes, and the mystery of the ring's owner drives the story from there. It is a compact piece of Harte's mining-camp manner: one object, one conscience, and a settlement watching.
govdocs-archive_org-TheTruthAboutGalileo: Garbled text of a work defending the Catholic Church's side of the Galileo case makes up this file; its author is not identified in the text. It opens on the schoolbook account of the Inquisition seizing and torturing the astronomer, the version the book sets out to correct as lies and errors. Much of the capture is damaged, so the argument survives only in part. It is kept as found, a partial record of Catholic apologetics on a famous trial.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AllenMarkFBIHSC: Researcher Mark Allen spent years prying assassination records loose through Freedom of Information suits, and his name labels several files in this archive. This set holds FBI records tied to the House Select Committee on Assassinations concerning ZR-RIFLE, the CIA's cryptonym for its executive action capability, its assassination program. The papers are kept as released, part of the record of how private researchers forced the files open.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAChemBioWar_C:
Eugene L. Meyer of the Washington Post reported on a secret the Army had kept in the Maryland woods. In 1969, Army testers sprayed fluorescent particles over a forest on the Eastern Shore, again and again, to study how such material falls and spreads.

The tests, run 115 times, measured fallout patterns for chemical and biological warfare studies, using tracer particles in place of actual agents. Stories like Meyer's brought the domestic test programs into the open during the 1970s, when the country learned how much experimenting had been done at home. The article is preserved as part of that exposure record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimMisc:
The National Insider, a tabloid weekly, ran an article in April 1970 under a shouting headline: The Ugly Truth About the John F. Kennedy Conspiracy Fiasco! Its target was New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison and his prosecution in the Kennedy assassination case. The byline is garbled and cannot be recovered.

Garrison's case had collapsed in court the year before, and tabloids fed on the wreckage. The Insider's version sold the story as farce, not investigation. The article preserves that tone as evidence of how the Garrison affair looked in the checkout-line press.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HoltRinehartAnd: An FBI memorandum dated July 1, 1966 was addressed to Cartha DeLoach, one of J. Edgar Hoover's top deputies. Only a fragmentary text survives, and its subject cannot be recovered from what remains. The record preserves the date and the recipient, a senior headquarters official, so the memo stands as a dated fragment of Bureau paperwork from the summer of 1966.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HooverJEdgarKen:
A newspaper article covers a new novel called The Chancellor Manuscript and its shock theory. The book mixes real people and events with an invented premise: that J. Edgar Hoover withheld vital information about the Kennedy and King assassinations. Fiction borrowed the director's secret files for its plot.

Hoover's real habit of keeping damaging files made the premise easy to sell. A thriller built on his silence let readers enjoy suspicions that nonfiction could not prove. The article preserves the book's arrival, when a novel about the director's secrets was itself news.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HurleysWhiteCar: A fragment of a trial transcript preserves the State describing a witness's observation. Mrs. Elizabeth Copeland had seen a small white automobile near the Campe Amusement Company. Which trial the fragment comes from is not identified in the record. What survives is the prosecution putting her sighting of the white car into the courtroom record, one detail in a larger case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinEdwardGov:
A news article reports a charge by Governor Edward Martin of Pennsylvania against a federal Resources Board report. Martin said the report planned a postwar 'New Order' for the United States. In his telling, the plan would create a caste system. The article's own publication is not identified in the file.

The fight belonged to the war years, when Americans argued over how much planning the peace would bring. A governor attacking a planning board in the language of caste and fascism shows the heat of that argument. The headline pairs the charge with 'fascists,' the era's strongest word. The clipping preserves the accusation and its terms, if not the report's answer.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NixonRichardMHi:
A magazine article looks at Richard and Pat Nixon and their family one year after his resignation. The Nixons were living in isolation at San Clemente, California. The publication and the author are not identified in the file. The piece belongs to the first round of 'what became of them' reporting after Watergate.

Resignation in disgrace made Nixon the first president to leave office that way. Reporters wanted to know how the family lived with it. The article describes a household cut off from the public life it had filled for decades. As evidence, it preserves the tone of 1975 curiosity: sympathy, disbelief, and attention to daily routine at the western White House turned exile.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RamousBar_Ramou:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum about the Ramous Bar in Dallas. The bar was connected in his notes to a man named John Edward Roddenberry and to discussion groups he calls 'Ham-Ham.' Weisberg works through who was seen there and what was said. He ends with a caution: in July 1963, the man described was not Oswald.

Bars and the men in them fill assassination research, because Oswald's double is the theory's oldest resident. Weisberg, usually the accuser, here plays corrector, ruling a lookalike out of his own inquiry. The memo shows that discipline at work. It names the place, the people, and the date, and then refuses the easy identification those names invited.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TorontoStar_Tor: Harold Weisberg wrote to Mr. Worthington at the Toronto Star on February 25, 1974, pitching his books. Weisberg spent years promoting his attacks on the Warren Commission to editors in the United States and Canada. The letter is part of that long campaign for attention and reviews. It shows a self-published researcher working the press, one editor at a time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ValleeThomasArt: Edwin Black reported in the Chicago Independent in November 1975 that four men may have taken part in a plot to kill President Kennedy in Chicago. The alleged target trip was a November 1963 visit, and Thomas Arthur Vallee was the man arrested in that case. Black's article argues Chicago nearly saw the assassination first. It remains a central text for the Chicago plot claim.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WandasBar_Wanda: From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers. An obscure item, complete, filed. A bare file, kept as issued. Subject: government records. nsia-WandasBar Wandas Bar: the made public government document, captured as titled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergHaroldM: nsia-WeisbergHaroldMilitary Weisberg Harold Military: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-qanon-part-01-1-fbi-: On August 13, 2018, the FBI opened a preliminary investigation connected to QAnon, and the opening electronic communication survives in the bureau's FOIA Vault. QAnon was then a growing online conspiracy movement. An opening EC is the formal paper that starts a case and states its basis. The document shows the moment a fringe internet story became a federal file. The library holds it without taking a stance.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_aa83_The:
During NATO's Able Archer 83 exercise, some Soviet leaders feared a real first strike was hiding inside a drill. The Soviet Side of the 1983 War Scare tells that autumn from Moscow's point of view.

Drawing on declassified records, the briefing book reports that a Politburo member warned the exercise could mask an actual attack. Soviet forces raised their readiness in answer. Told from the other side of the wall, the story changes a familiar exercise into a two-sided scare, in which each side's caution looked like the other side's threat.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_henry-ki:
In the mid-1970s the nuclear worry in Washington was Seoul, not Pyongyang. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 582, published in March 2017, as the first part of a series. Declassified documents show the Ford administration working to stop South Korea's bomb ambitions.

Ford officials aimed to inhibit development of a South Korean nuclear explosive capability. South Korean officials resisted at first, since their government wanted the option as insurance. The posting draws lessons for today's proliferation fights. Its main one is historical: a determined Washington once talked a close ally out of the bomb, using pressure the public never saw.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_korea-nu: The US and the North Korean atom threat: made-public records in this National Security Archive briefing-book capture. How Washington tracked Pyongyang's bomb. A single capture, dated. From the archive set. For those tracing the long standoff.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico_N:
In April 2026, reports said two CIA officials had died in northern Mexico after an operation to dismantle a clandestine drug laboratory. Claire Dorfman edited this briefing book, posted that month, on the tensions the deaths raised. Its title frames the problem: new challenges, old playbook.

The flashpoint was the extent of American involvement in Mexico's drug war. Direct United States operations on Mexican soil carry a long and sensitive history between the two countries. The posting uses the reported deaths to examine a partnership that keeps returning to the same methods. Readers get a current case set against decades of documented cooperation and friction.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Atomic Energy Commission planners once studied whether nuclear weapons could be made clean, and what nuclear war would do to the natural world. Their project built on work from the 1950s and early 1960s by a National Security Council subcommittee. That group ran net evaluations of a war's effects on both superpowers.

The Commission supported that work but wanted a more holistic approach, meaning the whole environment, not just blast damage. Studying the ecology of nuclear war in official files feels modern, yet the questions are sixty years old. The record shows early official curiosity about fallout, climate, and ecosystems as war effects in their own right.

How the Strategic Air Command Would Go to Nuclear War: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records.

A new official State Department history covers national security policymaking in the Carter presidency. It gives detail on two sensitive subjects: nuclear targeting and continuity of government between 1977 and 1980. Continuity work plans how the government survives a nuclear attack.

Official histories digest thousands of files into a narrative that later researchers trust and cite. One covering targeting choices and survival plans for the Carter years fills a real gap, since both subjects stayed classified for decades. The posting's value is the spotlight: it tells readers which parts of the new history carry the newest light, and why Carter-era decisions still frame later practice.

Few decisions remain argued about like the use of atomic bombs against Japan in 1945. This Archive briefing book posts declassified documents on that decision and on the end of World War II. It presents the record rather than a verdict.

Documents are the firmest ground in this debate. Memos and minutes show what decision makers knew, what alternatives they weighed, and what they expected the bombs to achieve. Readers who approach the set directly can test the claims made by every side since: about invasion casualties, Soviet entry, and Japanese surrender. That is the collection's purpose, evidence first.

In January 1968 an American B-52 bomber carrying nuclear weapons crashed near Thule Air Base in Greenland. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2025, on that crash and its impact. It is the second part of a series on the United States and Greenland's nuclear history.

A bomber crash scattering nuclear material on Arctic ice created a political crisis with Denmark, which governed Greenland and barred nuclear weapons in its territory. The cleanup and the diplomacy both left long records. This part of the series follows the accident's effects, which reached from local contamination fears to the rules for American forces in the far north.

Since 1945 no American president has ordered a nuclear weapon used in war, a restraint scholars call the nuclear taboo. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in November 2017, on presidents and that tradition. It publishes declassified records on how the taboo held across administrations.

Evidence here is brief, so the description stays with the theme the title states. The taboo is not a law; it is a habit built by decisions in Korea, Vietnam, and other crises where use was considered and refused. Documents from those moments show the habit forming. For readers, the set explains a non-event, the dog that never barked, which shaped the nuclear age as much as any test.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nunn-lug:
The Chernobyl reactor disaster of 1986 is retold here through the eyes of the Soviet leadership itself. Svetlana Savranskaya, Sarah Dunn, and Brooke Lennox edited this briefing book, number 681, published in August 2019. It is the first volume of a two-part publication, with Alla Yaroshinskaya's help.

Declassified documents detail the highest-level reactions, the cover-ups, and the private critiques. Sources include Politburo notes, diaries, and protocols never before translated into English. That translation work is the posting's gift: readers can watch a secretive system absorb a catastrophe in its own paperwork, from the first confused reports to the management of blame.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness: Divided Berlin was the front line of the Cold War intelligence war, full of tunnels, defectors, and double agents. This briefing-book page examines the CIA's covert role in that secret war for Germany, through recently declassified documents, as its subtitle states. The evidence supplied here is the title and subtitle alone, so the operations covered cannot be listed. The subject is well chosen: no city concentrated the espionage contest like Berlin, and declassified records keep adding named cases to its legend.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber:
One year after the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, a National Security Archive cyber brief looked back at the digital side of that day. The brief draws on records about how the House protected its own data during the riot and how investigators later used online material to build their cases.

A statement by the House Chief Administrative Officer describes steps taken to guard House data while rioters were inside the building. Social media, the brief notes, served both sides: attackers used it to organize, and law enforcement used it as evidence. It also cites the Internet Covert Operations Program and data scraped from Parler, which officials said could help prevent future violent protests. The result is a compact record of how the internet shaped both the attack and the response.
history-of-florence-and-of-the-affairs-o:
Niccolò Machiavelli wrote his History of Florence on commission from the Medici, covering the city from its earliest times to the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent in 1492. Machiavelli treats Florence as a case study in faction: nobles against people, guilds against magnates, and party hatred renewed in every generation. The revolt of the Ciompi wool-workers, the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici, and wars with Milan and the papacy fill his middle books.

Unlike The Prince, the History argues in narrative, showing how internal division invites foreign masters. Machiavelli praises civic virtue wherever he finds it and blames Florence's habit of destroying her own citizens. The unnamed translator of this edition keeps the old Bohn version's plain style. It remains a founder's text of modern political history.
julius-caesar:
William Shakespeare's Julius Caesar appears here under its old title, The Tragedie of Julius Caesar. The opening scene puts Flavius and Murellus on stage with a crowd of commoners. Both men scold the workers for walking out on a labouring day. They ask why the men wear their best clothes without signs of their trades.

A carpenter is questioned first, then a cobbler answers with wordplay about his trade. Flavius asks where the carpenter's leather apron and rule have gone. The cobbler calls himself a poor match for a fine workman, yet jokes on. That sharp, funny street talk sets the tone before Caesar himself appears.
king-lear:
King Lear, by William Shakespeare, is laid out here through its cast list and later scene headings. Lear is named King of Britain at the head of the cast. His daughters are Goneril, Regan, and Cordelia, listed in age order. Albany and Cornwall appear as husbands to the two elder daughters.

The scene list for Acts Three to Five moves across wild and wartime ground. Settings include a heath, a hovel, and Gloucester's castle rooms. Later scenes shift to the French camp near Dover and nearby fields. The British camp near Dover hosts the final act scenes. Edgar, Edmund, Kent, Gloucester, and the Fool complete the main cast.
l-p-m-the-end-of-the-great-war:
J. Stewart Barney published the novel L.P.M.: The End of the Great War in 1915. Its opening chapters are called The Man and the Hour and The One-Man Secret. A third chapter follows a crossing with royalty.

Barney wrote while the First World War was still being fought. His story imagines how one secret might end that war. The frontispiece shows a count facing an American in a tense scene. It is a wartime adventure built on hope for a sudden, dramatic peace. The initials of the title hide the secret at the plot's heart. Suspense rests on who knows the secret and who must not.
life-and-letters-of-john-gay-1685-1732-a:
Lewis Melville published this life and letters of John Gay in 1921. Gay, who lived from 1685 to 1732, wrote The Beggar's Opera. A sketch by Sir Godfrey Kneller serves as the frontispiece portrait. Daniel O'Connor of Great Russell Street issued the London edition.

Melville had already written lives of Thackeray, Sterne, and Cobbett. Here he turns that practiced hand to an earlier English wit. Letters mix with narrative to show Gay among his contemporaries. The book suits readers curious about the age of Pope and Swift. Melville's earlier lives covered Sterne, Beckford, Cobbett, and the Berry sisters. Thackeray studies made his name before he turned to Gay.
men-in-war:
Andreas Latzko wrote these six linked stories about soldiers in the First World War. The book is dedicated, pointedly, to friend and foe alike. Its scenes open in the garden of a war hospital in a small Austrian town. That was in the autumn of the war's second year.

The stories follow men off to war, through first battle, wounds, and the trip home. Trains carry fresh troops one way and the bleeding wounded back the other. Latzko shows fear, pain, and madness rather than glory. Few war books of its time argued so plainly that war itself was the enemy.
michael-strogoff-or-the-courier-of-the-c:
Michael Strogoff, the Czar's courier, is the hero of Jules Verne's Siberian adventure. The story begins during a splendid ball at the New Palace. A dispatch reports that the wire beyond Tomsk has been cut. Tartar forces are moving, and Siberia is slipping from the Czar's control.

Strogoff is sent east with a warning meant for the Czar's brother in Irkutsk. His road crosses steppe, river, and enemy-held country. He travels under a false name, hiding his mission from everyone. Verne fills the journey with escapes, betrayals, and tests of endurance that made the novel a lasting favorite.
morning-star:
H. Rider Haggard dedicated this romance of old Egypt to Dr. Wallis Budge. Budge kept the Egyptian and Assyrian antiquities at the British Museum. Haggard's letter calls himself an amateur beside Budge's mastery of Egyptian language and lore. Budge advised him to leave the story exactly as it was.

Haggard's author's note defends his boldest device. In the tale, a queen's Ka, or Double, stays occupying her throne. Meanwhile the queen herself journeys and adventures abroad. Egyptian theory, he argues, gave the Ka an existence of its own, immortal and awaiting resurrection. The novel builds royal romance on that ancient belief in the double self.
mr-punch-s-history-of-the-great-war:
Charles Larcom Graves edited this Punch record of the Great War, issued in 1919. Punch was Britain's famed comic magazine. The book went through seven printings in a few months. A verse note thanks the writers and artists who made it.

The prologue recalls Punch watching wars since its early days. It names the Crimea, the Mutiny, and the rise of Prussia. Then it turns to five hard years just ended. Cartoons, jokes, and verse carry the tale of the home front. The mix shows how Britons used humor to bear fear, loss, and hope.
my-second-year-of-the-war:
Frederick Palmer reports his second year at the front in this 1917 book. Dodd, Mead issued it in New York. Palmer had written My Year of the Great War before it. Chapter one takes him back to the front at once.

Verdun and its sequel fill the next long chapter. Then comes the Somme: the blow, its first results, and its guns. Palmer tells of Contalmaison stormed and a brigade that went through. A Canadian innovation earns its own chapter. The book is a skilled American reporter's plain record of the war's hardest year, seen from the lines.
nasa-tm-19660012950-observed-ultraviolet:
Spectrograms of Mars, taken from a sounding rocket, give the measure of how strongly that planet reflects ultraviolet light. On March 19, 1965, an Aerobee rocket rose from White Sands Missile Range carrying the instrument. Its camera was built by the Kollmorgen Corporation, with a special wide-field design. A grating spread the light into a spectrum for study.

Ultraviolet light never reaches the ground, so rockets must carry the camera above the air. How much ultraviolet Mars reflects reveals facts about its thin atmosphere. Comparing the measure with a model atmosphere tests that model. The flight was brief, but the spectrograms preserved data no ground telescope could gather at the time.
nasa-tm-19680017356-review-of-recent-bal:
Thomas N. Canning, Michael E. Tauber, and Max E. Wilkins of Ames Research Center review ballistic range tests on ablating cones in this paper. The question is whether smooth laminar flow can cover much of a blunt cone during very fast entry. Such cones model capsules returning through the atmosphere at extreme speeds.

Models ablating in the range matched mass transfer rates expected in real flights up to high entry speeds. Early data compared total ablated mass with laminar and turbulent predictions. Measured values fell between those two extremes. Triangular wedges of heavier removal marked where turbulent flow began. The review tracks how those patterns grew as test conditions changed.
nasa-tm-19680023899-analysis-of-launch-w:
Larry A. Manning, Byron L. Swenson, and Jerry M. Deerwester, of NASA Headquarters' Mission Analysis Division, wrote this September 1968 memorandum, TM X-1651. They analyze launch windows from circular orbits for representative round-trip missions to Mars. A launch window is the limited span when a ship can leave and still reach Mars with the fuel it carries.

The summary opens by defining representative windows and the velocity changes each one demands. Chapters lay out the method, from orbit geometry and quick thrust burns to costly plane changes. Later sections work a typical case, covering Earth and Mars windows and how sensitive fuel needs are. Appendices treat three-burn trips and departure needs at both planets.
nasa-tm-19690024022-hydromagnetic-observ:
K. W. Ogilvie and L. F. Burlaga of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this July 1969 paper, numbered X-616-69-303, on hydromagnetic observations in the solar wind. Plasma and magnetic data from Explorer 34, carrying a Goddard-University of Maryland experiment, supply the evidence. Hydromagnetics treats the solar wind, the Sun's streaming outflow, as a magnetized fluid with waves and shocks of its own.

At boundary surfaces between wind streams, the field ran parallel to the surface, as tangential discontinuity theory requires. Sharp speed jumps there hinted at gliding motions, with indirect signs of swirling instability. Several traveling shocks obeyed the standard shock relations well. Sudden storm commencements, they find, almost always trace to such shocks, while smaller sudden impulses have mixed causes.
nasa-tm-19690027648-variations-in-electr:
N. C. Maynard and J. P. Heppner of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this August 1969 preprint, X-642-69-374. They report variations in electric fields measured from polar orbiting satellites. New probe techniques, using long antennas on rockets and satellites, had just made such direct field measurements possible. The paper asks what fields exist above the poles, and how they change.

Theory pictured the fields as smooth convection patterns tied to ionospheric currents. Maynard and Heppner note that smooth patterns explain only the gross behavior. Smaller scale irregular structure must be understood to explain auroral shapes and forms. Barium cloud drift studies tracked field changes over time, while the satellite probes map changes over space. Their purpose is defining the fields' true character more closely.
nasa-tm-19700026395-mission-d-as-504-104:
Mission D has its final Apollo abort summary in this Houston internal note, dated January 2, 1969. The mission flew with vehicle AS-504. Mission D was Apollo 9, the first crewed test of the lunar module in Earth orbit, flown on the Saturn 5 rocket.

The document gathers crew procedures into a single reference for training. It covers normal Saturn 5 flight, aborts, and abort entries, with the basic text matching the procedures crews would actually use. A limits table divides the climb into abort modes by time and altitude, from low altitude escape tower modes onward. Later modes run through full lift entry, service module engine returns, and an engine burn all the way to orbit.
nasa-tm-19710003362-magnetic-susceptibil:
D. E. Hegland and D. R. Behrendt of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It measures how strongly several rare earth compounds answer a magnetic field. The compounds join rare earth metals with selenium or tellurium.

The team cooled the samples close to absolute zero and raised the field step by step. Most of the compounds showed signs of antiferromagnetic order, the authors report. In that state, atomic magnets line up in opposed ranks and cancel out. One compound showed its own magnetization at the coldest settings. In most cases the pull per atom matched the value figured for the charged rare earth ion.
nasa-tm-19710004288-a-comparison-of-sphe:
Raymond M. Hicks and William R. Harper Jr. of the Ames Research Center ran this wind tunnel study. It compares two shapes used to trip a boundary layer into turbulence at supersonic speeds. The shapes are small spheres and small triangles on a flat plate.

A trip forces the smooth flow next to a surface to turn rough at a chosen point. The team placed the trips at varied distances from the plate's leading edge. Tests ran in the Ames supersonic tunnel across several Mach numbers. Knowing which shape trips the flow best helps engineers design test models. It also keeps tunnel data honest about real flight.
nasa-tm-19710012088-three-investigations:
Klaus Schocken of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this memorandum, NASA TM X-64577, dated February 11, 1971. It gathers three investigations of the interstellar medium, the thin gas spread between the stars. One study concerns how X-rays fade as they cross space. The catalog record also points to the physical state of a hydrogen cloud.

The abstract opens with a clear claim. X-ray weakening in space is concentrated inside clouds of gas. Outside the clouds, the weakening is far smaller. That pattern tells astronomers where the absorbing matter sits. Work like this helped map the structure of gas that stars and planets later form from.
nasa-tm-19710014565-numerical-analysis-o:
Raymond C Clerkin of the Lewis Research Center wrote this April 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2270. It works through the numerical solution of two linked integral equations. One equation is of Volterra type and holds a singularity that needs special care. The other is of Fredholm type and contains a principal value term.

Clerkin explained how to compute the principal value part. He tested the technique on a hard integral whose answer was already known. Reaching a stable repeated solution took two fixes. He lowered the relaxation factor and forced one function to stay smooth near the singularity. Such methods support later computer work on tough math problems.
nasa-tm-19720022951-diminiode-performanc:
Arthur L Smith, Richard B Lancashire, Eugene J Manista, and James F Morris of the Lewis Research Center mapped this tiny power device in September 1972, as NASA TM X-2587. The device is a diminiode, a miniature thermionic diode that turns heat into current. Its emitter was a tantalum alloy called ASTAR-811C. The collector used niobium with one percent zirconium. A guarded collector kept the readings clean at the edges.

A computerized facility swept and recorded the performance map. The gap between the hot emitter and collector stayed fixed. It measured only a quarter of a millimeter across the flat faces. Such small diodes served as test vehicles for bigger converters. Their maps showed how new electrode materials behaved. The work continued a long Lewis program in thermionic power.
national-association-for-the-advancement:
Published in New York in April 1919, Thirty Years of Lynching in the United States counts mob killings from 1889 to 1918. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People issued it from its office at 70 Fifth Avenue. The price on the title page was fifty cents.

Front pages list other pamphlets the group had printed on the same crime. Titles name President Wilson's 1918 statement on mob violence and probes in Georgia counties. Other items cover East St. Louis, Memphis, and Abbeville. Put together, the book gave readers a plain record of lynching and of early work against it.
native-races-and-the-war:
Josephine E. Butler published Native Races and the War in London in 1900, while the South African war was still being fought. She dedicated the book to her children and grandchildren. Her opening chapter asks why yet another book on the South African question was needed.

Butler argues that future peace must rest on justice for coloured men as well as white men. She recounts the Transvaal from 1877, its taking by Britain, and its release in 1881. She prints speeches and protests by native chiefs, and proof about slavery there. Her case rests on hearing the native races themselves.
neutral-rights-and-obligations-in-the-an:
Robert Granville Campbell published this study in 1908, growing out of work in the political science seminary at Johns Hopkins. It forms part of a larger study of the causes of the Anglo-Boer War. Its theme is the law that bound countries not fighting in that war.

Britain first treated the fight as too small to wake the neutrality laws of others. By late November it put the war on a plain footing as a war. It dated the start to the Transvaal ultimatum of October 11, 1899. Campbell asks how far the United States met its neutral duties. He then turns to European governments, and to trade with neutrals in wartime.
new-latin-grammar:
Charles E. Bennett, Goldwin Smith Professor of Latin at Cornell, wrote this New Latin Grammar for students. Copyrights run from 1895 through 1918, and Bennett dated his preface at Ithaca on May 4, 1918. He calls the book a revision of his 1908 grammar, with no deep changes.

Bennett added an opening account of how the Latin language began and grew. He hoped keen pupils would find it useful and pleasing. Small fixes sharpen rules, and syllable division now follows Roman practice, he says. Long vowels are marked in more endings than before. An index at the back points to the sources of examples used in the syntax.
on-war:
Carl von Clausewitz wrote this classic study of warfare. Colonel J. J. Graham translated it into English. The first edition of that translation appeared in 1874. A revised London edition followed in 1909, in three volumes. Colonel F. N. Maude added introduction and notes.

The introduction calls war force used for a political object. It praises Clausewitz's deep, philosophical analysis of war. Events since Waterloo follow his teachings, the editor claims. Napoleon first taught the lessons Clausewitz set in form. No book has shaped military thought more strongly. The notes liken his work to what Darwin did for life science. Two famed battle fields gave that same hard lesson, he adds.
othmar: Othmar is a novel by Ouida, pen name of Maria Louise Ramé. This new edition was printed in London in 1886. The catalog dates the work 1885. Its title page carries a line from Lytton: I fear Life's many changes, not Death's changelessness. The hosted sample, however, shows only that title page. It also shows the start of a contents list giving chapters by page number. No line of Ouida's prose appears. This note records only what the front matter establishes.
our-navy-in-the-war: Lawrence Perry's Our Navy in the War is a wartime account of the United States Navy in the First World War. Scribner's published it in October 1918. The book is dedicated to Secretary of the Navy Josephus Daniels. The hosted sample shows the title pages and that dedication. A photograph shows the Atlantic fleet steaming in line. One contents line begins: the Navy's first experience with the German U-boat. No narrative chapter appears.
peace-theories-and-the-balkan-war:
Norman Angell, author of The Great Illusion, published Peace Theories and the Balkan War in 1912. The Balkan War had just broken out, and critics said events had refuted his famous argument. The book opens by quoting a Sheffield speech of Winston Churchill asking who would still say that force is never a remedy.

Angell answers his critics and tests his theory against the new war. He had argued that conquest no longer pays in a world bound by trade and credit. The pamphlet is a defence written under fire, while the war it discusses was still being fought.
pellucidar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens Pellucidar with a prologue told by a big-game hunter. The narrator is packing for northern Africa when a letter postmarked Algiers pulls his departure forward by twelve days. The letter draws him into the story that follows, of the hollow world inside the Earth.

Pellucidar continues the adventures of David Innes, who returns to that inner world to free its human tribes from the reptilian Mahars. The chapter titles promise lost travellers, cave-prisons, raids, and conquest and peace. It is pulp adventure at full stretch, with a stone-age world lit by a central sun.
plays-of-near-far:
Lord Dunsany's Plays of Near and Far was first printed in December 1922 by G. P. Putnam's Sons, in London and New York. The edition was limited to five hundred copies. A front list names his earlier books, from The Gods of Pegana to The Chronicles of Rodriguez.

The contents page opens with The Compromise of the King of the Golden Isles, on page one. The Flight of the Queen follows, a longer play that starts on page twenty-one. A third piece, Cheezo, begins on page sixty-five, as the list shows.
robur-de-veroveraar:
Jules Verne's Robur the Conqueror appears here in Dutch, as Robur de Veroveraar, in the Wonderreizen series from Elsevier of Amsterdam, dated 1915. Its heading dates the tale itself to 1886. Chapter one opens with two pistol shots and a cow hit in the back, though she had no part in the quarrel.

The two duelists, an older Englishman and a younger American, had fought over a tune heard in the air near Niagara. One swore it was Rule Britannia, the other Yankee Doodle. A witness proposes that it was both, and the party goes to breakfast at the Goat Island hotel, between the falls, over eggs, ham, and floods of tea.
ruth-fielding-in-the-great-northwest-or-: Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding in the Great Northwest, or The Indian Girl Star of the Movies, issued in New York by Cupples and Leon. Emerson is named as author of Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill, Ruth Fielding in the Saddle, and Ruth Fielding Down East. A picture shows timbers pouring down a bluff behind the heroine.
secret-chambers-and-hiding-places-histor:
Allan Fea collected tales of priest holes, hidden rooms, and secret passages in great houses across England. Fea had written before on King Charles the Second's flight and on King Monmouth. Eighty pictures show the halls and hiding places, and this printing is the third, revised one.

Chapters visit Hindlip Hall, Harvington, Boscobel, and Moseley, among many other houses. Fea tells how priests hid from hunters and how kings fled after lost battles. Gunpowder Plot men also figure in the tales. House by house, the book turns brick and oak panels into a record of fear, loyalty, and daring escapes.
springhaven-a-tale-of-the-great-war:
R. D. Blackmore sets Springhaven in the days of one man's sway. Its sub-title calls it A Tale of the Great War. The book is dated 1887. Chapter I bears the head When the Ship Comes Home. England then trusted to the vigor of one man. A world of foes stood against her. No part of her coast faced more peril than Springhaven's vale. Yet the quiet village bore itself without fear.

Blackmore paints the valley as a place made for rest. Deep rich meadows fill it. Thick leaf cover and old trees shut out noise. No glaring chalk mars the scene. No grim sandstone faces the vale. Upland crests of soft gray lias rise above. Orchards thrive on their slopes. Quick rills lace the slope with twisted silver. Twenty small waters meet in the vale. They run to the bay that takes their name.
stonewall-jackson-and-the-american-civil:
Colonel G. F. R. Henderson wrote Stonewall Jackson and the American Civil War, a two-volume life with portraits, maps, and plans, introduced by Field-Marshal Viscount Wolseley. Volume I follows Jackson from West Point through Mexico in 1846-47 and his years at Lexington from 1851 to 1861.

The contents then run through secession, Harper's Ferry, First Manassas, and the famous Valley campaign, with chapters on Kernstown, Winchester, and Cross Keys and Port Republic. The Seven Days, Cedar Run, Second Manassas, Sharpsburg, and Fredericksburg close the volume. Henderson, himself a soldier and author of tactical studies, treats Jackson as a case study in bold, fast generalship.
tales-of-war:
Lord Dunsany published Tales of War in 1918, while the First World War still raged, gathering short tales told in plain, close voices. The first piece, The Prayer of the Men of Daleswood, sets the tone for the whole book.

Daleswood held just twenty houses, and some thirty men of age to serve all went to war in one platoon. Luck held for them till March, when a vast German push broke the line at their side. Readers get war seen from small lives and tight bonds, where fate, prayer, and chance weigh as much as guns in Dunsany's spare, grave tales.
tarzan-and-the-jewels-of-opar:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar, a Tarzan novel in twenty-four chapters that returns to the lost city of Opar. Chapter heads trace a road to Opar, an altar of a flaming god, a jewel room, and flight and theft.

The tale opens with Lieutenant Albert Werper, a Belgian officer saved from disgrace only by a grand name. Sent to a lone Congo post in place of a court trial, he broods through six months of dull exile. From there the plot pulls in Arab raiders, the priestess La, and Jane Clayton in peril. Readers get lost-city gold, jungle fights, and Tarzan swung between beast and man.
the-adventures-of-akbar: Flora Annie Steel wrote The Adventures of Akbar. Byam Shaw drew its plates. William Heinemann of London printed it in 1913. Front pages carry ads for companion volumes. They name The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett. They name Alice's Adventures in Wonderland as well. A dedication in verse then starts. A plate shows baby Akbar on a dry sand bank. He sits up and rubs his eyes.
the-american-indian-as-participant-in-th: A full contents list maps Annie Heloise Abel's 1919 history. Its title is The American Indian as Participant in the Civil War. Abel is styled a doctor of philosophy. She is also professor of history at Smith College. Chapters open with the Battle of Pea Ridge. They move to Lane's Brigade and refugees in southern Kansas. Then they trace the first Indian expedition and the march to Tahlequah. Later heads cover Generals Pike and Hindman in dispute. Closing heads treat military matters of 1864 and 1865.
the-art-of-war:
Baron de Jomini, general and aide-de-camp to the Emperor of Russia, wrote this study of war, here in a new edition with added parts and maps. Captain G. H. Mendell and Lieutenant W. P. Craighill of the United States Army turned it from the French; the version was first published in 1862.

Their preface weighs the two faults a translator must dodge: clinging word for word to the source, or writing too freely and losing the sense. Jomini's translators say they aimed at plain English, neither cutting nor adding to his ideas, with no show and no carping. They offer the book to readers who study war for instruction.
the-audacious-war:
Clarence W. Barron published his war book in Boston and New York in 1915, with Houghton Mifflin, after copyright entries in 1914 and 1915. A third impression followed the February 1915 publication. Facing the title is a long poem headed with a question about what would happen if war were fully unleashed.

Verses in that poem picture guns, blocked ports, hungry cities, and sunken warships. Fields are trampled, streams are fouled, and schools of art and trade lie in ruins. The poem asks what such ruin could satisfy, calling the outcome a kind of self-destruction for civilised life, before Barron's prose treatment begins.
the-boer-in-peace-and-war: Arthur M. Mann wrote The Boer in Peace and War, put out in London by John Long in 1900. Mann had also written The Truth From Johannesburg. The book has sixteen plates, and their list gives a clear hint of its scope. Boer mounted police form the front plate. Wagons bring wool to an early market in Johannesburg and cross a river, and a Boer home and a Boer family are shown. Majuba Hill, a Boer camp, the Raadzaal or hall of law, and President Kruger's house close the list.
the-boy-scouts-in-front-of-warsaw-or-in-:
Colonel George Durston wrote The Boy Scouts in Front of Warsaw, or In the Wake of War, book twenty of the Boy Scout Series. The first chapter is called The Disappearance. It is the fifth of August, and Warsaw has fallen. Torn by bombs and wrecked by great shells, the city lies in ruins.

Warsaw was taken on the third of August, and in two days most of her folk have vanished. The rich have fled to the low part of town, leaving fine houses to the flood of troops. Durston places the city on the left bank of the Vistula, in a fair plain. Her streets twist and curl like snakes, and her old houses bear barred doors and solid shutters. Harm fell worst in those packed low streets, he says, yet fine state houses and palaces in the new part lie in ruins too.
the-boy-tar:
Captain Mayne Reid opens The Boy Tar, dated 1859, with an old man who speaks to his boy audience in his own voice. Philip Forster lives in a quiet sea town on the shore of a very large bay. The folk live by fishing more than by trade.

Forster was born in the town and means to die there, yet his neighbors know him least of all. They call him Captain, or the Captain, though he was never a captain in army or navy. He was master of a merchant ship, a skipper, and the name is their courtesy. He lives alone up the shore and walks each day to the pier with a telescope. He grants he has traveled far and reads much, but says his learning is self-taught.
the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-part-: Charles Farrar Browne, who wrote as Artemus Ward, is the author behind part 2 of this seven-part Gutenberg series. The part's theme, per the record title, is war. Nothing of Browne's text is present, though: the header fills the whole space with copyright notices and donation appeals.The front matter is all a reader gets in this record.
the-conquest-of-fear:
Basil King wrote The Conquest of Fear, here printed with a new introduction by Henry C. Link. The contents trace a chain of eight chapters, each linking one idea to the next. First come fear and the life-principle, God and his self-expression, the mind of today, and the world as it is. A false god of fear follows. At last come the fear of death and a full life.

King opens by saying fear dogged most of his waking life, and he takes that to be true for most people. He recalls childhood dread of bedtime, then fear of school, then the grown-up dread of waking to duties left undone, mistakes made, and losses no one saw coming.
the-crisis-of-the-naval-war: Admiral of the Fleet Viscount Jellicoe of Scapa wrote The Crisis of the Naval War, dated 1920, with eight plates and six charts. Its contents cover Admiralty organization and the changes of 1917, the submarine campaign early that year, anti-submarine work, and the bringing in of the convoy system. Later chapters treat the entry of the United States, patrol craft and minesweeping, the Dover Patrol, and Admiralty production. Only the title page, contents, and the start of the plate list are present here.
the-devil-s-own-a-romance-of-the-black-h: Randall Parrish subtitled The Devil's Own a romance of the Black Hawk War. The A. L. Burt edition was published by arrangement with A. C. McClurg under an October 1917 copyright, with a frontispiece by the Kinneys captioned with a girl asking if the man is dead. The contents open with chapters at Old Fort Armstrong, on furlough, on the Beaucaires' history, and a girl at bay at Judge Beaucaire's home. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-diverting-history-of-john-gilpin-sho:
William Cowper's comic ballad The Diverting History of John Gilpin appears here as one of R. Caldecott's picture books, dated 1878. John Gilpin, a respected London linen draper and train-band captain, has given his wife no holiday in twenty years of marriage. She plans a trip to the Bell at Edmonton to mark their wedding day.

The chaise holds his wife, her sister, and the children, so Gilpin must ride behind on a borrowed horse. Cowper's brisk verses and Caldecott's drawings turn a simple outing into a famous wild ride. The poem stays light, swift, and fond of its hero.
the-dreamer-a-romantic-rendering-of-the-:
Mary Newton Stanard's The Dreamer, printed at Richmond in 1909, calls itself a romantic rendering of the life story of Edgar Allan Poe. Stanard tells the reader she used a storyteller's right to dress sparse facts in full scenes. She holds the tale true in spirit if not in letter, and puts Poe's own words in his mouth where she found them.

An epigraph from Poe's Eleanora praises those who dream by day. The book traces Poe through Richmond, school, debt, and fame. It suits readers who want Poe's sad life told as a novel.
the-edda-volume-1-the-divine-mythology-o:
Winifred Faraday's The Edda: The Divine Mythology of the North came out at London in 1902. It stands as Popular Studies number twelve. A note on spelling opens it. Norse thorn and eth become th and d. Vowel length marks are dropped. She calls the Icelandic Eddas the sole home-tongue record of Germanic heathendom.

The Elder Edda holds some thirty poems, mythic and heroic. They stand in a thirteenth-century book. That book came to light in Iceland in 1642. Faraday retells the gods' world for plain readers: Odin, Thor, and the doom of the gods. Her short study still serves as a first guide.
the-edda-volume-2-the-heroic-mythology-o:
Winifred Faraday's The Edda: The Heroic Mythology of the North, Popular Studies number thirteen from 1902, forms a sequel to her study of the gods. Her note sends readers back to that book for its preface and source list. She opens with the heroes of Germanic legend: Sigemund, Aetla, Eormanric, Theodric, and Weland the Smith.

Old English poems name such heroes in a word or two, with no tale attached, since English verse turned to saints and Scripture. Iceland kept the full songs. Faraday traces Sigurd, the Nibelungs, and other hero cycles for plain readers.
the-extraordinary-adventures-of-arsene-l:
Maurice Leblanc wrote these tales of Arsene Lupin, the gentleman-burglar, first gathered in 1907. Nine stories make up the book, and the contents name arrests, escapes, a queen's necklace, a black pearl, and a locked safe among them.

The first story opens aboard the fast liner La Provence, where wireless news now links a ship to shore. Word comes that Lupin is among the passengers, and the calm social world of the crossing turns tense. Charm, nerve, and disguise drive the plots, and in the last tale Sherlock Holmes himself turns up, too late.
the-germ-thoughts-towards-nature-in-poet:
The Germ was the short-lived magazine of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, first printed in 1850 and here reprinted in facsimile in 1901. William Michael Rossetti, who edited the first run, adds a long introduction.

Rossetti grants he has written much on the Brotherhood's early days, above all on his brother Dante Gabriel and his sister Christina. He sets out to give the magazine its due: its members, allies, and aims in a British art world he calls dull and lifeless in 1848. Turner alone stood great and old. Against that age the young brotherhood set fresh sight, truth to nature, and poems and tales of their own.
the-great-boer-war: Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Great Boer War. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The chapters open with The Boer Nations, The Cause of Quarrel, and The Negotiations. They open with The Eve of War. Then they follow the fighting: Talana Hill, Elandslagte, and the battle of Ladysmith. They name Lord Methuen's advance, Magersfontein, Stormberg, and Colenso. They name the siege of Ladysmith, Spion Kop, and Paardeberg. They end with Roberts's advance on Bloemfontein. No chapter text is present.
the-history-of-the-thirty-years-war:
Frederick Schiller wrote The History of the Thirty Years' War. The Rev. A. J. W. Morrison translated it from the German. A preface for a collected edition of Schiller's works frames the book. The preface argues that Schiller was fit by nature for history. He was no less fit for history than for drama, it says. His clarity and impartial judgment are praised.

A contents summary for Book I follows. It lists the general effects of the Reformation. It also lists the revolt of Matthias. Later topics include the Union and the League. Troubles in Bohemia turning to civil war close the list. The summary shows a war built from faith, crowns, and rival leagues.
the-homeric-hymns-a-new-prose-translatio:
Andrew Lang made a new prose translation of The Homeric Hymns. Essays, literary and mythological, stand with the translation. David Price transcribed the text from the 1899 George Allen edition. The book is dedicated to Henry Butcher. The dedication calls the book a token of a long friendship. Introductory essays open with the so-called Homeric Hymns.

Lang quotes a hard judgment from Baumeister at the start. The existing collection is of unknown editorship, date, and purpose. Lang weighs why short preludes were kept while longer poems were lost. He also weighs what the Alexandrian critics show about the hymns. Thucydides and Pausanias give further evidence. Brief hymns, he notes, served rhapsodists as preludes.
the-iron-game-a-tale-of-the-war: Henry F. Keenan inscribed this tale of the war to Bernard John McGrann. The dedication praises McGrann's manliness, modesty, and worth. It is dated New York, March 25, 1891. A printing of 1898 carries the book. A verse epigraph fronts it. A heavy, solemn cloudy column marches over green fields there. The fields spread like a table for the iron game's dice. Only the front matter and first contents entries are present here. The story itself does not appear. Book I is called The Caribees. A boy in blue opens it.
the-land-of-deepening-shadow-germany-at-: D. Thomas Curtin reported from inside Germany during the First World War, and his book appeared in 1917 with a dedication to Lord Northcliffe. Only the title page and full contents are present here, listing twenty-eight chapters on propaganda, spies, police rule, war work at Essen, and Berlin life. The reporting itself, chapter by chapter, does not appear in this record.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Suetonius wrote the Lives of the Twelve Caesars, biographies of Rome's first emperors, in Alexander Thomson's translation as revised and corrected by T. Forester. This opening volume is prefaced by an account of Suetonius himself. His father was a Roman knight who commanded a legion for Otho. Suetonius was born near the end of Vespasian's reign. He rose to be secretary under Hadrian, then was dismissed in the year 121 over alleged familiarity with the empress Sabina.

The preface also explains his method, using his friendship with the younger Pliny as a character witness. He writes memoirs rather than history, dwelling more on personal habits and conduct than on public events. That plan shapes the life of Julius Caesar and every life that follows in the set.
the-parlor-car:
A one-act farce, The Parlor-Car, appears here as transcribed from The Sleeping Car and Other Farces, in the 1911 Houghton Mifflin edition. No author is named in the pages present. The scene is a parlor car on the New York Central Railroad, late on an autumn afternoon. A gentleman sleeps alone in the car, hat over his eyes and a newspaper across his lap.

The conductor brings in Miss Lucy Galbraith, heavily veiled and tearful, with the porter carrying her wraps and bags. She cannot ride backwards and chooses a seat by a window. The porter tells her the train runs more than four hours late after a freight wreck near Rochester, and that Schenectady is the next stop. Her distress sets the farce moving.
the-path-of-a-star:
Mrs. Everard Cotes, also known as Sara Jeannette Duncan, published The Path of a Star in 1899. Chapter One opens with an actress entering a room. She pushes the portiere aside with a curved hand, head forward and eyes inquiring, though she knows exactly who is there. Her morning gown's train takes bold folds as she bends over Laura Filbert on a bamboo sofa.

"You poor thing!" she cries, taking Laura's hand. Laura answers that she is happier than her visitor, much happier. Her bare feet nestle in a coarse rug, and her eye rests on a tall Owari vase in the room's cheap magnificence. Duncan sets two unlike women face to face.
the-pride-of-palomar:
Peter B. Kyne's novel The Pride of Palomar was published at New York by Cosmopolitan Book Corporation in 1922. H. R. Ballinger and Dean Cornwell drew the illustrations, and the frontispiece shows Don Miguel Farrel. Kyne is named as author of Kindred of the Dust. A dedication letter to Frank L. Mulgrew of the Bohemian Club in San Francisco stands at the front.

In the letter Kyne admits the finished book is not what he wanted or planned it to be. It holds, he hopes, a few faint echoes of the spirit of old California. That California was already vanishing when he was born. Mulgrew had hunted local colour with him for The Valley of the Giants in the north. Last summer he did the same in the south, unearthing more tender sentiment than Kyne could use. For that reason, Kyne tells him, the book is peculiarly his friend's own.
the-riddle-of-the-rhine-chemical-strateg: Victor LeFebure is named as author on the edition header. The header gives the title on chemical strategy. It covers strategy in peace and in war. An April 1998 release date appears there too. Only that edition header is present on these pages. Its general notices appear with it. No part of the argument itself appears here. Nothing about its chapters can be told from these pages alone.
the-scarlet-car:
Richard Harding Davis's The Scarlet Car contains three stories, according to its contents. They are The Jail-Breakers, The Trespassers, and The Kidnappers. The first story opens on the morning of the Harvard and Yale game. A trip in Winthrop's car had long been arranged.

Peabody pictured himself in the back with Miss Forbes. Her brother Sam would ride in front with Winthrop. Peabody's invitation was necessary because he was engaged to Miss Forbes. Sam could act as chaperon for his sister. Winthrop stops the car at her door at nine o'clock. He is in love with all the world that morning. Beatrice Forbes is engaged to another man, he reflects. She is not married yet, though. The scarlet car chugs and trembles outside her house.
the-shape-of-fear: Elia Wilkinson Peattie's The Shape of Fear and Other Ghostly Tales opens with a transcriber's note. The note lists small corrections made to the text. Wedgwood's spelling and a superfluous word are among them. The contents then names eleven tales. The title story comes first, followed by On the Northern Ice. Their Dear Little Ghost and A Spectral Collie follow. The House That Was Not and Story of an Obstinate Corpse also appear. An Astral Onion closes the list. No tale text itself is present in the portion shown.
the-short-line-war:
Samuel Merwin's The Short Line War lays out a railroad fight in twenty-three chapters. Jim Weeks opens the book, and Mr. McNally goes to Tillman City next. Politics, Judge Black, and Judge Grey all get chapters. Somebody loses the books partway through. A capture at Brushingham and McNally's expedient follow. Katherine decides near the end, before the winning of the road and the surrender.

Chapter one traces Jim Weeks's fighting stock. His great-grandfather Ashbel was born in Connecticut in 1748. He migrated to New York in 1770 and settled among the Oneida Indians. Danger suited him, Merwin writes; he sniffed at it like a young horse. He fought beside Herkimer in the Oriskany Creek ambush. He served with the army of the North through Yorktown. Then he married and returned home among the Oneidas.
the-skipper-and-the-skipped-being-the-sh:
Holman Day subtitled The Skipper and the Skipped as the shore log of Cap'n Aaron Sproul. Harper and Brothers published it in February 1911. Day also wrote The Ramrodders and King Spruce. A frontispiece shows the skipper telling of the glorious, fascinating sea.

Chapter one seats Cap'n Sproul by a bedside. His uncle, One-arm Jerry, lies there with dimming eyes. Sproul was late skipper of the Jefferson P. Benn, the text explains. Jerry pleads his case in a continuing conversation. It ain't being a crowned head, but it's honourable, the sick man insists. The scene opens the shore log on that deathbed appeal, with the old skipper listening.
the-soul-of-the-war:
Philip Gibbs wrote this account of the opening phase of the Great War, with an introduction prepared for the electronic edition by Anthony Langley. Ten sections move from foreboding and mobilization through retreat and invasion. They reach the last stand of the Belgians, the soul of Paris, the soldiers of France, and the men in khaki.

The first chapter asks who can lay bare the soul of England in the July days when the menace of a great, bloody war suddenly reached ordinary people. Gibbs compares the shock to a sinner convicted at a revival meeting, going home a changed man in a changed world where even the clock's ticking sounds different.
the-story-of-a-plush-bear: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a plush bear was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, under a 1921 copyright. Only the title pages and a publisher's list are present here. The list shelves the book among the Make Believe stories. The Sawdust Doll and the White Rocking Horse stand beside it. The Nodding Donkey and the China Cat follow. The bear's own adventures do not appear.
the-story-of-sugar: Sara Ware Bassett, author of companion stories of lumber, wool, leather, and glass, wrote this industrial tale for young readers, illustrated by C. P. Gray and inscribed to her cousin William Pittman Huxley, with thanks to the American Sugar Refining Company. Only the opening pages and contents appear in this record. The contents list six chapters. They run from Colversham and a narrow escape onward. Sugaring off and the refinery follow. A family tangle closes the list. The tale itself does not appear.
the-tale-of-cuffy-bear: Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time tale of Cuffy Bear was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1915, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title pages appear in this record, with two lists. One list names the Sleepy-Time tales. Frisky Squirrel and Tommy Fox stand there. Fatty Coon, Billy Woodchuck, and Jimmy Rabbit follow. Peter Mink, Sandy Chipmunk, and Brownie Beaver come next. Paddy Muskrat stands beside Cuffy. The heading of a contents list follows. Cuffy's own adventures do not appear.
the-united-states-since-the-civil-war: Charles Ramsdell Lingley, professor of history at Dartmouth College, published The United States Since the Civil War in 1920. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the history's chapters do not appear. Twenty-five chapters begin with Reconstruction and its aftermath, then move through Grant's time and the economic foundations of a new era. Headings cover Hayes, the overturn of 1884, transportation control, and laissez faire. Later chapters trace diplomacy, the wage earner's rise, imperialism, Theodore Roosevelt, Wilson, and the World War.
the-upas-tree-a-christmas-story-for-all-: Florence L. Barclay, author of The Rosary, published The Upas Tree with G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1912. The subtitle calls it a Christmas story for all the year, and F. H. Townsend supplied an illustration. Only the opening front matter is present in this record, so the story itself does not appear. A dedication to V. C. B. precedes a contents list for part one. Its three chapters are titled Which Shall Speak First, The Sob of the Woman, and Helen Takes the Initiative.
the-valley-of-fear:
Arthur Conan Doyle divides The Valley of Fear into two parts, The Tragedy of Birlstone and The Scowrers. Part one gives Sherlock Holmes a warning, a discourse, a country-house tragedy, and a solution across seven chapters. Part two crosses to Lodge 341 at Vermissa, following a bodymaster, the darkest hour, and the trapping of Birdy Edwards.

Chapter one opens in Baker Street banter, with Watson protesting that Holmes can be a little trying at times. Illustration captions scattered through the front matter quote dramatic lines about witchcraft, lunatics, and whispered warnings. A second record in the library carries the same novel in another edition, with matching contents and the same opening exchange.
the-war-after-the-war:
Isaac F. Marcosson published The War After the War with John Lane in New York and London in 1917, dedicating the volume to Lord Northcliffe. A signed photograph of Lloyd George, captioned Let freedom win, faces the title page. Copyright lines reach back to 1916 magazine publication.

His foreword reckons nearly three years of Europe drenched in blood and torn by bitter strife. Millions have been killed or maimed, and billions in property have gone up in smoke and ruin on the altar of the Great War. The tumult must subside, Marcosson writes: smoke will clear, scarred fields will green again with spring, and fighting hosts will return to peaceful pursuits as time passes.
the-war-chief-of-the-ottawas-a-chronicle:
Thomas Guthrie Marquis wrote The War Chief of the Ottawas for the Chronicles of Canada series, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton. Published at Toronto in 1915, it forms volume fifteen of thirty-two and chronicles the Pontiac War. Contents chapters promise the siege of Detroit, the fall of the lesser forts, and the relief of Fort Pitt.

Chapter one opens with rejoicing across the Thirteen Colonies in September 1760, when Montreal capitulated. Bonfires flamed and prayers rose for deliverance from a foe that had harried frontier settlements for a century. French armies were beaten by land and fleets by sea, Louisbourg lay razed, and British flags flew over Quebec, Montreal, and Niagara. Marquis sets that triumph as the calm before Pontiac's storm.
the-world-war:
Logan Marshall's The World War promises a history of the nations and empires in the Great Conflict. His preface recalls how Americans first heard of Sarajevo. Archduke Francis Ferdinand and his wife were assassinated on June 28, 1914. Americans felt regret for the aged Emperor Francis Joseph. Nobody imagined the shots would hurl Europe into war within a week. Marshall stresses the suddenness and enormity of that plunge.

Church bells, he writes, were drowned by cannon roars. A shudder of terror ran through the world. The preface then turns back through history for causes. Readers get an early American attempt to explain the war. Its tone mixes shock, sympathy, and search for meaning.
three-years-war: Christiaan Rudolf de Wet published Three Years' War with Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1902. A frontispiece by John S. Sargent and four plans and a map accompany the book. De Wet dedicated it to his fellow subjects of the British Empire. Contents begin with going on commando as a private burgher, then Nicholson's Nek and besieged Ladysmith. A fourth chapter promises his appointment as a fighting general. The title pages and opening contents are what is present here, so de Wet's Boer War memoir itself is not shown.
two-months-in-the-camp-of-big-bear: Two Months in the Camp of Big Bear tells the life and adventures of Theresa Gowanlock and Theresa Delaney, written by the two women themselves. The contents run from leaving Ontario through a massacre, life with the Indians, and cooking for a large family, to rescue and the journey home. Part two turns to youth, marriage, and the North-West troubles. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the captivity narrative itself does not appear.
un-doc-haile-selassie-s-address-on-inter:
Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia gave this address for International Education Year in 1970. The United Nations had set 1970 aside for schooling, with UNESCO in the lead. Two thirds of the world's people still lacked any real chance to learn. Ethiopia had made study a top claim on its funds.

He notes that Ethiopia set up its own schools commission in June 1968, before the UN vote. That body was charged to chart aims and growth for teaching at home. He praises adult reading drives and the prizes won by Ethiopian groups. Learning, he tells his people, is a duty shared by every family. New schools must turn out the skilled hands growth needs.
under-the-great-bear: Kirk Munroe's Under the Great Bear, published at New York in 1901, takes its title from an early Labrador voyage account in which Ursa Major seemed likely to fall from overhead. The contents open with graduation and an offer of employment, then a boy alone on a life raft, the French shore question, and bluffing the British navy. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the Labrador adventure itself does not appear.
valentine-m-clutchy-the-irish-agent-the-:
William Carleton opens Valentine M'Clutchy, the Irish Agent in the town of Castle Cumber. He sketches it in a few strokes. Two long streets cross, and lanes of mud cabins stretch out on each side. A church, a prison, a courthouse, and a Catholic chapel stand in the town. An old stone cross stands in mid street. A fair green at the west end holds two fairs a year.

Chapter one sets its scene on a fair day in December. Snow and hard frost had held for nearly three weeks. Now black clouds mass over the white ground. The chapter's heading promises an Irish pair, a marriage proposal, and an under agent. It also names an old squire and a union lord. Carleton writes of the land agent system that ground Irish tenants. He starts where that system met daily life.
walker-s-appeal-with-a-brief-sketch-of-h:
Henry Highland Garnet brought David Walker's Appeal back into print at New York in 1848. He joined it with a brief sketch of Walker's life and with his own address to the enslaved people of the United States. His preface, signed at Troy in April 1848, tells how the task arose. High esteem for Walker's memory, a general desire to keep the Appeal in reach, and leave from Walker's widow all played a part.

Garnet ranks the pamphlet high. It was among the first appeals in behalf of freedom, he writes. It was the boldest and most direct made in the early days of the antislavery reform. A companion record of the same edition carries the same title page and preface. This copy stops at the heading of the life sketch, where the other runs on a few lines. The Appeal itself, Walker's 1829 call to the enslaved, follows the sketch in both.
war-and-the-future-italy-france-and-brit:
H. G. Wells wrote War and the Future from tours of the fronts in 1916. His contents divide the book in three. The war in Italy, on the Isonzo front and in the mountains, fills the first part. The western war fills the second, with ruins, new arms, and tanks. A long look at how people think about the war fills the third. Pacifists, conscientious objectors, the riddle of the British, and the war's ending all get chapters.

The first essay, The Passing of the Effigy, takes up the tour of the front itself. After months when even war correspondents were shut out, both sides found that opinion mattered more in this struggle than in any before. Opinion bloomed at home on rumor. Wells reports a war fought with words and images as much as with guns, and a public being taught to watch it.
what-is-coming-a-forecast-of-things-afte:
H. G. Wells published What Is Coming? in 1916, while the Great War still raged. The book tries to forecast the world that will follow the war. Its contents cover the war's end, nations in collapse, and a new map of Europe. Other chapters ask how far Europe will move toward socialism.

Wells opens by saying that prophecy can be a game or a grave task. Science, he argues, trains the mind to see what is already taking shape. Some things can be known with near trust, like tides and seasons. Others rest on weaker signs. Readers watch a famed writer test his method on law, schools, and women's gains.
where-no-fear-was-a-book-about-fear: Arthur Christopher Benson's Where No Fear Was is represented here by its contents and a long quote, with none of his essays present. Benson published the book about fear in 1914. The contents move from the shadow and shapes of fear to its use. Chapters then trace fear through childhood, youth, middle age, and old age. Named chapters treat Dr. Johnson, Tennyson, Carlyle, and Charlotte Bronte. The quote comes from Pilgrim's Progress, where Christiana sees an ugly thing on the road.
white-jacket-or-the-world-on-a-man-of-wa:
Herman Melville wrote White-Jacket, or The World in a Man-of-War. A note dated New York, March 1850, tells his source. In 1843 he shipped as an ordinary seaman on a United States frigate in the Pacific. He served more than a year and was let go when the ship came home.

His time and notes aboard went into the book, Melville says. The contents start with the jacket itself and a homeward bound chapter. Later parts sort the crew into ranks and name Jack Chase, a famed sailor. Melville shows the closed world of a warship, its ranks, rules, and punishments. Readers meet naval life from the lower deck.
why-we-are-at-war: The pages here give a publisher's note and contents for Why We Are at War, with Woodrow Wilson's messages themselves not yet shown. Harper and Brothers printed the book in May 1917. It gathers Wilson's messages to Congress from January to April 1917. The contents list a call for a world league for peace, the break with Germany, and a request for power to act. The war message of April 2 and the proclamation of April 6 follow.
william-lilly-s-history-of-his-life-and-: Only title pages and a plate list are present here for William Lilly's history of his life and times, so the memoir itself does not appear. Lilly wrote the account himself at age sixty-six, for his friend Elias Ashmole. It covers the years 1602 to 1681. The work was printed from his manuscript in London in 1715. This copy is a reprint for Charles Baldwyn dated 1822. The plates list two portraits of Lilly, plus Dr. Simon Forman and John Booker.
with-lee-in-virginia-a-story-of-the-amer:
G. A. Henty wrote With Lee in Virginia, a story of the American Civil War, for young readers. His preface, addressed to his dear lads, says the war holds a special pull for the English. Two parts of a kindred people fought, and the weaker side held out for four years. Ill-fed and ill-clad regiments faced a foe with more men, the sea, and Europe's factories behind it.

Henty notes that the rights of the case still draw dispute. The South claimed a right to leave the Union; the North denied it, and arms settled the point. Early war spared the people, he says, while later years brought wide ruin. Lee's Virginia campaigns carry the tale. Honor and hardship fill Henty's southern scenes.
won-by-the-sword-a-tale-of-the-thirty-ye:
G. A. Henty wrote this story of the Thirty Years' War as a sequel in spirit to The Lion of the North. His preface recaps the war's first phase. Gustavus and Wallenstein died, and Sweden lost at Nordlingen. Chancellor Oxenstiern then drew France into the fight. Richelieu saw that Austria, backed by Spain, could crush France if France stayed out.

France took Sweden's leading role and won. Henty credits two great captains, Conde and Turenne, who differed in style yet worked in harmony. One was careful with lives, the other reckless. Their campaigns frame the hero's adventures in war-torn Germany.
young-knights-of-the-empire-their-code-a:
Sir Robert Baden-Powell wrote these scout yarns in 1917 to teach character and good citizenship. His foreword calls the tales further pictures of ideas already set out in Scouting for Boys. Pictures alone do little good, he warns. Boys must turn the ideas into daily habit. Adults must encourage that practice, the foreword insists.

The opening explains the young knight idea. Old knights defended weaker people and lived by a code of chivalry. Thousands of boys across the British Empire now follow the scout law in that spirit. Stories then show the code at work. Readers get adventure with a clear moral frame.
